[The visualization of the weapons is as follows: "In the left [upper hand] and the right [upper hand], [the first]; in the left [lower hand] and the right [lower hand], the others. Having performed this meditation on the weapons, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement of the hands, offer the recitation to the Goddess, and prostrate. This is the *Durgā-mantra*. Now, the *Mahiṣamardinī* [mantra].

The Durgā mantra is: *Mahiṣamardinī svāhā*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this eight-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Mārkaṇḍeya on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Mahiṣamardinī in the heart. Then, having uttered "For the attainment of all desired goals," [one recites]: "O Mahiṣamardinī, huṃ phaṭ, salutation to the heart; O enemy of Mahiṣa, subdue him, huṃ phaṭ, svāhā to the head; O Mahiṣa, neigh at the enemy, huṃ phaṭ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-locks."

*Ṭ mahiṣaṃhanahanadevi huṃ phaṭ kavacāya huṃ mahiṣasūdani huṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ.* Having thus assigned these five-limbed mantras to the fingers from the thumb to the little finger— excluding the *astra* and *netra* [mantras]— and to the heart and other limbs, one should perform the meditation as follows: "Like the sun, adorned with a crest-jewel and earrings, with a third eye upon her forehead, seated upon the severed head of Mahiṣa, holding a conch, discus, sword, shield, arrow, bow, trident, and also a pointing finger..."

Having meditated on the sister [Durgā], who has the moon as her crest-ornament, holding the *tarjanī* (threatening) finger with her own arms—the *tarjanī* mudrā being formed by the right index finger raised upward, the next pair held downward, the following pair held downward, and the others held at the side—one should perform the recitation (*japa*). At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed the five-limbed ritual placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) and offered the merit of the recitation to the Goddess, one should prostrate. This *tarjanī* mudrā consists of the single index finger raised upward while the remaining fingers are extended downward. Now follows the Durgā mantra for recitation: *Oṃ durgai durgai rakṣasi svāhā*. With this ten-syllable mantra, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having performed the *nyāsa* of the Ṛṣi and others thus: "Salutation to Nārada, the Ṛṣi, upon the head; salutation to Virāṭ, the Chandas, upon the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Japadurgā upon the heart"; and having performed the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* with: "Oṃ, salutation to the Heart; Durge, Svāhā to the Head; Durge, Vaṣaṭ to the Crest (Śikhā); Rakṣaṇi, Huṃ to the Armor (Kavaca); Svāhā to the Eye; Vauṣaṭ; [with the entire mantra] Phaṭ to the Weapon (Astra)"; one should meditate [upon her]: "Her splendor like the ocean, wearing a moon as a crown, holding a discus, mace, sword, and lotus in her lotus-hands..."

One should bow to Jayadurgā, who possesses three eyes, rides upon a lion, and holds a rosary (*akṣamālā*) and a trident (*triśūla*) in her left hands—starting from the upper left and ending with the lower left—and a conch (*kṣam*) and a weapon (*vāyudha*) in her right hands—starting from the upper right and ending with the lower right. Having meditated thus, at the conclusion of the recitation performed according to one's capacity, one should perform the *ṛṣyādi-vinyāsa*, offer the recitation to the Goddess, and bow down. Now follows the second [section]: the mantras for the recitation of Durgā.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the twelve-syllable mantra: *Oṃ namo durge durge rakṣaṇi svāhā*, one should perform the previously mentioned *ṛṣyādi-vinyāsa* and *viniyoga*.

Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantra parts beginning with "Oṃ namo hṛdayāya namaḥ," one should perform meditation, recitation (*japa*), and so forth as before, starting with [the verse] "Seated upon a throne, with the luster of emerald," and so on.

Now follows the third *japa-durgā* mantra: "Oṃ namo bhagavati jvālāmālini gṛdhra-gaṇa-parivṛte svāhā. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-two-syllable mantra, one should offer salutations: to the sage Dīrghatamas at the head; to the meter Kakup at the mouth; and to Japadurgā at the heart.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra "To which deity... (*yā devatāyai...*), and having performed the five-limbed placement (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*) with the mantra words beginning with "Oṃ namaḥ hṛdayāya namaḥ," and having performed the meditation (*dhyāna*) to be described later beginning with "She who has the luster of a dark cloud" (*nīlāmbhodhara-kāntim...*), one should perform the *ṛṣi*-placement and so forth at the end of the recitation (*japa*), offer [the merit], and prostrate. This is the third [section]. Now, regarding the Durgā-mantra for the wielder of the trident (*śūlin*): having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the fifteen-syllable mantra "Jvala jvala śūlini duṣṭagraha huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should place [the ṛṣi] on the head: "To the Ṛṣi Dīrghatamas."

"Obeisance to Mukheka-kupchandas; obeisance to the goddess Śrīśūlinī Durgā in the heart. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the application (*viniyoga*) is stated as follows: "O Śūlinī! O Durgā! You who are worshipped by gods and *siddhas*! Protect me, O Nandinī! O Great Mistress of Yoga (*mahāyogeśvarī*)! *Hūṃ Phaṭ*. Obeisance to the Heart. O Śūlinī, granter of boons! O Goddess worshipped by gods and *siddhas*! ... [etc. Svāhā to the Head. O Śūlinī, dweller of the Vindhya! O Goddess worshipped by gods and *siddhas*! ... [etc. Vaṣaṭ to the Crest-lock (*śikhā*). O Śūlinī, crusher of the immortals! O Goddess worshipped by gods and *siddhas*! ... [etc. Huṃ to the Armor (*kavaca*). O Śūlinī..."

One should meditate upon her—[the goddess] who delights in hand-to-hand combat and terrifies [her foes]—while assigning the five-limbed mantras, beginning with *devasiddha* and ending with *astrāya phaṭ*, to the fingers from the thumb to the little finger (excluding the index finger), and to the heart and other limbs.
She has the luster of a dark blue cloud, wears a crown of the moon, and is mounted upon a lion. With her auspicious hands, she holds a trident, an arrow, a sword, a discus, a bow, and a noose;
she is attended by four maidens carrying a scimitar and a shield, and she is adorned with various ornaments. She has three eyes.

One should worship Śūlinī Durgā; having meditated upon her weapons starting from the lower right hand up to the lower left hand, and having performed the *japa* as much as possible, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other limbs (*ṛṣyādika*) at the conclusion of the recitation, offer the *japa* to the Goddess, and prostrate. This is the mantra of Śūlinī Durgā. Now, for the mantra of Navadurgā: "Arise, O Puruṣikī! Why do you sleep? A danger has come upon me. Whether it be possible or impossible, O Blessed One, pacify it for me, svāhā! Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-seven-syllable mantra, [one should proceed].

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by saying "Salutation to the forest-dwelling seers (*āraṇyaka-ṛṣis*)" on the head, "Salutation to the *anuṣṭubh* meter" on the mouth, and "Salutation to the deity Śrī Navadurgā" on the heart, and having stated the application (*viniyoga*), one performs the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) on the hands and the heart with the following mantras:
"Arise, O Person!"—*namaḥ* to the heart; "Why do you sleep?"—*svāhā* to the head; "Fear has come upon me"—*vaṣaṭ* to the tuft (*śikhā*);

"If it is possible or impossible"—*huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*); "O Blessed One, pacify that for me"—*vauṣaṭ* to the eyes; *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*). Thus, the six limbs are assigned to the hands and the heart.

One should meditate upon the auspicious Durgā, who dwells in the forest of the heart, as follows: she is seated upon a golden lotus, possessing the brilliance of a flash of lightning; she has three eyes, and in her lotus-like hands she holds, in order, a mace, a conch, a sword, a shield, a bell, and a discus. She wears garments of a rising golden luster, her crest-jewel is a shimmering gem touched by the moon, and at her sides and above her are two noble lions. Having thus meditated on her weapons—the first pair being held upwards and the other pair downwards—one should perform the recitation (japa), and at its conclusion, assign the Ṛṣi and other limbs [of the mantra].

"May she protect me"—this is the mantra of the Nine Durgās. Now, for the mantras of Lakṣmī: having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the single-syllable mantra "Śrīṃ," one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as follows:

"Salutation to the sage Bhṛgu on the head; salutation to the Nivṛt metre on the mouth; salutation to the goddess Śrī on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable 'Śaṃ' on the private parts; salutation to the power (śakti) 'Draṃ' on the feet; salutation to the pin (kīlaka) 'Raṃ' on the navel. Having stated the application (viniyoga), one should perform the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) assignment: "Śrāṃ to the heart, salutation; Śrīṃ to the head, svāhā; Śrūṃ to the tuft, vaṣaṭ; Śraiṃ to the armor, huṃ; Śrauṃ to the eyes, vauṣaṭ; Śraḥ to the weapon, phaṭ. Thus ends the six-limbed assignment.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should meditate [on the Goddess] as follows: she is seated upon a lotus; her eight hands—four on each side—are raised, displaying a pair of golden lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of granting boons (*vara*); she is like the snowy mountain (Kailāsa) in splendor; her slender body is being sprinkled by eight lordly elephants with their trunks raised, holding jars filled with nectar; she possesses great prosperity, wears a beautiful crown and silken garments, and has lotus-eyes. Having meditated thus, and having performed the *nyāsa* of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) on the hands at the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer [the prayer] and prostrate. This is the single-syllable mantra of Lakṣmī: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*. [Regarding the visualization: "The first [hand] is above the right [shoulder], the other is below the first on the left; the others are placed accordingly. Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas* each for the three [sections], one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the blessed Ṛṣi" on the head; "Salutation to the *Nivṛt* Anuṣṭubh metre" on the mouth; "Salutation to the deity Śrī Kamalā" on the heart. Then, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantra beginning with *Śrāṃ Śrīm*, one should meditate as follows: "Lakṣmī, who dwells upon a lotus, whose hands hold a pair of fresh lotuses and the *abhaya* gesture, is being sprinkled by four lordly elephants, dark as mountains of rubies, with waters from jars made of jewels rising from the ocean. May she protect us from sin."

Having meditated upon her as being served by hosts of *ḍāmaras*, with the first two [syllables] at the two upper lotus-feet and the other two at the two lower ones, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed the placement of the *ṛṣi* and so forth, and having offered the recitation, one should prostrate. This is the four-syllabled mantra of Lakṣmī. Now, the ten-syllabled [mantra]: *Namaḥ kamalavāsinyai svāhā*.

Having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to Dakṣa, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to the *Virāṭ* meter on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Kamalā on the heart."

Having stated the application (*viniyoga*), one should spread the root mantra over both hands. Then, one should perform the five-fold placement (*pañcāṅga-vinyāsa*) on the hands and heart as follows: "Oṃ *devyai* hṛdayāya *namaḥ*; Oṃ *padminyai* śirase *svāhā*; [Oṃ] *viṣṇupatnyai* śikhāyai *vaṣaṭ*;
[Oṃ] *varadāyai* kavacāya *huṃ*; [Oṃ] *kamalarūpāyai* astrāya *phaṭ*. Having performed this, one should meditate as follows:

"She who has the luster of a mass of lightning, whose hands grant a pair of lotuses and the gesture of fearlessness; she who, with the radiance emerging from her body, illuminates the cavity of the world; she who dwells upon a lotus, adorned with a girdle and a jeweled crown..."

May she, whose body is bent by the weight of the jar-like breasts of Lakṣmī and who possesses the beautiful splendor of the lotus-stalks, be present. The visualization of the weapon (*āyudha-dhyāna*) is as before. At the end of the recitation, having performed the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other elements, one should offer the recitation.

Now follows the twelve-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hsauḥ jagatprasūtyai namaḥ*. Having performed the three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) thus:

"Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart. Having performed this placement:

Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the hands and other parts as follows: *Aiṃ jñānāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Hrīṃ aiśvaryāya śirase svāhā*, *Śrīṃ śaktaye śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Klīṃ balāya kavacāya huṃ*, *Hsau vīryāya netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *Jagatprasūtyai namaste astrāya phaṭ*; one should meditate as follows:

First, one should remember a garden resplendent with all seasons, adorned with the leaves of *kapūra-kadala* trees swaying gently in the breeze, and [filled with] *aśoka*, *pāṭala*, and *nāga* [trees].

It was delightful with *kovidāra*, *mallikā*, *yūthikā*, *kunda*, and fragrant *madayantī* flowers; it was adorned with rows of *nāgabalī*, *mādhavī*, and *devadāru* trees, as well as *nameru*, *lavaṅga*, *vakula*, and *tilaka*. It was further beautified by *karṇikāra*, *candana*, and red *candana* trees, along with *vañjula*, *mātuluṅga*, auspicious *dāḍima*, and *takuca*; it was surrounded by *nālikera*, *kharjūra*, *pūga*, and *kuravaka* trees, and was filled with *mālatī*, *ketakī*, *jātī*, *pāraṃtī*, and *tulasī*, as well as *naṃdyāvarta* flowers.

The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon a beautiful great lake in its center— resplendent with *mānaka* trees blooming with flowers of all seasons, adorned with abundant *picumanda*, *mandāra*, and excellent *panasa* trees, as well as clusters of tall *śākhoṭa* and *kuṭaja* trees; radiant with the fragrance of blossoms touched by gentle breezes, it is graced on all four sides by bees dark as sapphire,

filled with the cries of peacocks, surrounded by *lakṣmaṇā* and cranes, shimmering with flocks of *varaṭā* swans, *cakravāka* ducks, and *kāraṇḍava* birds, and lovely with full-blown lotuses and *kahlāra* lilies.
The bright sandy shore was covered with *raja-ketakas*, blue lotuses, and other fragrant flowers, and adorned with groves of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) beautiful in all seasons.

In its center stood a pavilion with jeweled walls, radiant with the brilliance of the rising sun’s mass of rays, cooled by the nectar-like spray of the multitude of moonbeams, and most charming with shimmering golden ramparts. It was constructed from heaps of various gems, provided with four gates, composed of the nine precious jewels, and beautified by the splendor of its lofty arches. It was ever-new...

It possessed lofty gate-towers adorned with various great jewels; it was filled with clusters of banners and poles made of molten, refined gold; it shone with rows of pillars fashioned from great gems such as lapis lazuli; it was crowded with hundreds of windows crafted from refined gold; it was enchanting with thousands of half-banners shimmering on golden poles;

it was surrounded by pennants made of various kinds of silken cloth, gilded, and fitted with small bells; and it was encircled by auspicious canopies made of fine silk, radiant like the moonbeams of an autumn night, produced from diverse fabrics.

One should visualize a pavilion whose auspicious floor is adorned with golden bricks and jewel-studded slabs, and which is perfumed at its four doors by men using excellent sandalwood, aguru, camphor, musk, saffron, tamāla, and other fragrant substances. Within that, at the foot of a *pārijāta* tree, one should visualize a new lion-throne strewn with various heaps of gems;

upon it, one should contemplate the Goddess, possessing the radiant luster of the rising sun, adorned with a crescent moon on her head, resplendent with a pearl necklace, beautiful, and arrayed in jeweled ornaments.

She holds in her lotus-hands a fresh cluster of rice stalks; she possesses a pair of lotuses, the Kaustubha gem, and a face of beautiful smiles. Her three eyes are joined with the splendor of blossoming blue lilies from which her hair is loosened. Her two feet, adorned with tinkling anklets, resemble blooming red lotuses. She is made charming by a girdle-string shining upon the orb of her hips. Her waist is exquisitely beautified by three folds of skin. She is adorned with a circle of a deep-eddying navel-lake in her heart. Her full, elevated breasts are smeared with yakṣa-unguent, resembling the frontal lobes of an elephant.

She is resplendent with a necklace of pearls from the ocean of existence, wears a fine silken upper garment, and is beautifully adorned with flower garlands. Her limbs shine with emeralds and other gems set in refined gold;

her bracelets are bound with radiant rubies and golden lotuses. Her fingers are decorated with rings of various shimmering jewels, and she possesses a sweet, melodious voice like the warbling of a cuckoo. Her body is graced by diverse and wonderful ornaments, her smile is pure, and she is beautified by a jeweled ear-ornament as brilliant as the rising sun. Her ears are adorned with... [ear-pendants].

Her face was as beautiful as the moon, the lord of stars, free from blemish like the autumnal full moon; her lower lip-bud was radiant with the luster of shimmering coral and possessed the glow of ruby sprouts set against gold;

she was adorned with a row of lovely teeth shining like peaks; her eyebrows were more playful than the bow of the five-arrowed god of love; she bore a nose that shone like a blooming flower; her eyes were brilliant like blossoms; her forehead was graced by a beautiful lock of hair shaped like a crescent moon; and she wore a tilaka mark made of musk, rich with the fragrance of thick clouds.

One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī—the ultimate limit of the land of beauty, the birthplace of splendors, and the abode of the goddess of grace—whose lovely, dark-blue hair is uncurled and exceedingly glossy; whose beautiful hair scents the air with the fragrance of *pārijāta* flowers; who wears a crown of various jewels set in refined gold; and who is the very pinnacle of majesty. Then, beginning from the lower left hand and ending with the lower right hand, one should meditate on her weapons.

At the conclusion of the recitation performed according to one's capacity, one should again perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) for the hands, offer the recitation, and prostrate. Thus ends the twelfth [chapter].

The twenty-seven-syllable Lakṣmī-mantra: *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kamale kamalāye prasīda prasīda śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Dakṣa Prajāpati, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), in the mouth; salutation to Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the deity (*devatā*), in the heart. Then, having declared the application (*viniyoga*), one should recite: *Śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kamale śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* [for] the heart. *Śrīṃ* (3).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five limbs upon the heart and other parts with the mantra: *kamalālaye śirase svāhā*, *prasīda śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *prasīda kavacāya huṃ*, *mahālakṣmyai*, and *astrāya phaṭ*, one should meditate as follows: She possesses a luster red as vermilion, dwells in a lotus, and is the ground of exquisite beauty. With her lotus-like hands, she carries a vessel for offerings (*arghapātra*), a pair of lotuses, and a mirror. Surrounded by her handmaidens, she is adorned with a jeweled crown, necklaces, fine earrings, and a radiant girdle.

May that Lakṣmī, whose left arm rests upon her hip, be for your welfare. Having meditated on her starting from the lower left hand up to the lower right hand—or starting from the lower right hand [up to the left]—and having performed the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment) at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability, one should offer [the merit] and prostrate. Now follows the fourteen-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī: *oṃ śuddhavāsu menamo mahāśriyainamaḥ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this, and having assigned the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other elements as in the twelve-syllable Lakṣmī mantra, [one recites]: *oṃ hṛdayā* (heart)... *śuddhavāsa*.

Having performed the five-limbed assignment (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*) starting from the hands with: *Se śiraḥ*, *Namo śikhāyai*, *Mahāśriyai*, *Namaḥ astrāya phaṭ*, one should perform everything else, such as the meditation (*dhyāna*) mentioned immediately above.

Now follows the eleven-syllable mantra: *Yau tau mau bhaye śriye śrīr namaḥ*. (In this *Mahālakṣmī* [mantra], the meditation and so forth are similar to those previously described; the recitation (*japa*) is twelve hundred thousand times. One should meditate on this jeweled pavilion in the midst of a garden filled with various blossoming trees resounding with the cries of diverse birds, which shines with manifold splendors.

Therein, I worship Lakṣmī, who is seated upon a magnificent lion-throne provided with a pure silken cushion and adorned with excellent jewels; she has the moon as her crest-ornament, bears an auspicious cluster of blossoms on her left shoulder, and possesses three eyes; she holds a pair of lotuses and the beautiful Kaustubha gem. This meditation on Mahālakṣmī has been composed in brief from several verses found in the Meru Tantra. Regarding the visualization of the weapons, starting from the lower left hand and proceeding through the hands: [The description of the weapons follows.]

[One should meditate upon her] who resembles the sun, who bears four sprouts of rice (*śāli-mañjarikā*), a pair of lotuses, and the pure *śrī-kaustubha* gem; who wears a crown and ornaments of red hue, who is radiant with the three sacred fields (*kṣetra-traya*), and who holds a silken garment. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra "Obeisance to Pītāmbhā, the Fearless One," one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Obeisance to Jamadagni, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), at the head"; "Obeisance to the *triṣṭubh* metre (*chandas*), at the mouth"; "Obeisance to the deity Śrī Mahālakṣmī, at the heart. Then, [one should place]: "Obeisance to Pītāmbhā, the Fearless One, at the heart"; "Obeisance to the Heart"; "Pītāmbhā... at the heart.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by assigning [the mantras] to the hands, heart, and so forth—namely: *māutabhaye svāhā* to the head (*śiras*), *pautaumāutabhaye vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *pauta(o) huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *śriye netrāya vauṣaṭ* to the eyes (*netra*), and *śrīḥ namo astrāya phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*)—one should perform the remaining rites, such as meditation, as previously described. Then, for the fourteen-syllable mantra:

*padmaprabhe padmasudarī padmarṣe svāhā*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this root mantra (*mūla*). Then [assign]: *padmaprabhe hṛdayāya* (to the heart), *padmasudarī śira* (to the head), *padmarṣe śi*... [and so on].

Having performed the assignment of the five limbs (*pañcāṅga-vinyāsa*) with the mantras *khāṃ svāhā-kavaṃ* [for the heart], *samasta-mantrēṇāstrāya phaṭ* [for the weapon], one should perform everything else as previously described for the single-syllable mantra. Next is the *triśakti-lakṣmī* mantra; it should be understood as being the same as the *tripuṭā* mantra to be described hereafter. Now, for the *sāmrājya-lakṣmī* mantra: having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the six-syllable mantra *śrīṃ sakala-hrīṃ śrīṃ*, one should assign the limbs as follows: *śirase haraye ṛṣaye namaḥ* (salutation to the sage Hari at the head), *mukhe gāyatrī-chandasena namaḥ* (salutation to the Gāyatrī metre at the mouth), and *hṛdi śrīsāmrājya-lakṣmyai devatāyai* (salutation to the goddess Śrīsāmrājya-lakṣmī at the heart).

"Obeisance to Guhyeśa, the seed-syllable *Hrīṃ*; obeisance to the feet, *Śriṃ* to the power (*śakti*). Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) and declared the application (*viniyoga*), one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands, heart, and so forth:

"Obeisance to the heart, *Sakala Hrāṃ*; to the head, *Sakala Hrīṃ*; to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *Sakala Huṃ*; to the armor (*kavaca*), *Sakala Hraiṃ*; to the eyes, *Sakala Hrauṃ*—*Vauṣaṭ*; to the weapon (*astra*), *Sakala Hraḥ*—*Phaṭ*. Then one should meditate [upon the deity] who resembles the *atasī* flower, adorned with jewel ornaments, and holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus.

Having meditated upon her as holding a *śārṅga* bow and arrows in six hands, and adorned with the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) by the other two; [visualizing] the first pair on the left and right upper arms, the second pair on the left and right lower arms, the third pair on the left and right upper forearms, and the fourth pair on the left and right lower forearms—one should perform the recitation (*japa*). At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other limbs (*ṛṣyādi-vinyāsa*) and offered the oblation, one should prostrate. Now follows the seven-syllabled Lakṣmī-mantra: *namo brahmatanaye*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should assign the limbs: *namaḥ* to the heart, *brahmatanaye* to the head, *namaḥ śikhāyai* to the crest-lock, and *brahmatanaye* to the armor (*kavaca*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Caṃ" for the eyes, "Namaḥ" for the face, and "Istraṃ" for the heart—just as in the previously mentioned one-syllable *Lakṣmī* mantra beginning with meditation and so forth—one should proceed.

This concludes the *Lakṣmī* mantra. Now, the *Annapūrṇā* mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ namo bhagavati māheśvari annapūrṇe svāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-syllable mantra, one should perform the following placements:

"Salutation to Brahmā, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *Anuṣṭubh* meter (*chaṃdas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Annapūrṇā, on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable *Hrīṃ*, on the private parts; [salutation to] *Śrīṃ*, on the feet."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Oṃ *kīlaka* to the navel" and "Oṃ *kīlaka* to the heart," and having stated with palms joined, "The application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of equal prosperity in recitation (*japa*)," one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with "Hrāṃ to the heart, Hrīṃ Huṃ [to the head]," and so forth, and then meditate as follows: She resembles molten gold, has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, and wears a crown radiant with the luster of nine gems. She is reddish like saffron, clad in variegated garments, with eyes like those of a fish and three eyes. Her full, swelling breasts have the shape of golden jars; she is dancing.

Having meditated upon her—who is composed of bliss, who is supreme, whose eyes are tremulous with joy on her blissful face, who possesses a girdle and beautiful hips, who is eternally devoted to the distribution of food, and who is saluted by the Earth and Lakṣmī—one should perform the *karanyāsa* at the end of the recitation (*japa*). Having offered the *japa* to the Goddess, one should prostrate. This is the mantra of Annapūrṇā. We [the teachers] maintain that this sixteen-syllable mantra is devoid of the four seeds beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), and may optionally begin with either the *Māyā* (Hrīṃ) or the *Tārā* (Oṃ). Regarding the phrase "eternally devoted to the distribution of food" (*annadānaratā*), it should be understood that she holds a vessel in her left hand and the Goddess [of the vessel] in her right. After meditating thus and performing the *karanyāsa* at the conclusion of the *japa*, one should offer the merit of the recitation to the Goddess and bow down. This concludes the mantra of Annapūrṇā. We [the teachers] maintain that this sixteen-syllable mantra is devoid of the four seed-syllables beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), and may optionally begin with either the *Māyā* (Hrīṃ) or the *Tārā* (Oṃ).

The eighteen-syllable mantra beginning with *Māyā* (Hrīṃ) and *Tārā* (Oṃ), consisting of the seven syllables of *Vāgbhavī* and the eleven syllables of *Śākṣarī*, is formed as follows. Its seers (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes are as before. The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begin with *Hrīṃ* and so forth. Thus, there are four variations of this very vidyā. Now follows the procedure for the mantra of Annapūrṇā known as *Annaprada*: "O Food, O Great Food, come! O Lord of Food, grant me sustenance, svāhā! This twenty-two-syllable root mantra is used to perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). One should then offer salutations to Brahmā, the seer, at the head; to the *Atikṛti* metre, at the mouth; and so on.

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) with "Maḥ! To the deity Śrībhū, who is in my heart, namaḥ," and having declared the application (*viniyoga*) as "for the abundance of wealth and grain," one should touch the two thumbs at their inner ends with the joined palms while reciting the root mantra: "To the Heart, namaḥ"; on the two index fingers: "Grant me food, to the Head, svāhā"; on the two middle fingers: "O Lord of Food, to the Crest (*śikhā*), vaṣaṭ"; on the two ring fingers: "Bestow food upon me, to the Armor (*kavaca*), huṃ"; and on the two little fingers: "Svāhā to the Weapon (*astra*), phaṭ. Thus, [one performs the placement] excluding the eyes, up to the heart.

One should also meditate while placing [the mantras] upon compassion and the other virtues. One should contemplate at the break of day for the attainment of wealth, grain, and food: "In the milky ocean, upon the island of silver and gold, rich with gods and auspicious, adorned by groves of wish-fulfilling trees, seated before the two [deities] upon a jeweled throne—Earth and Lakṣmī—who repeatedly create heaps of riches for their devotees.

Having thus meditated, having performed the recitation according to one's ability, and having assigned the ṛṣis and other elements at the conclusion, one should offer the prayer and prostrate. This is the mantra of Annapūrṇā known as the "Bestower of Food."

[Thus ends the third chapter of the *Mantracandrikā*, composed by Gosvāmin Janārdana, son of Gosvāmin Jagannivāsa. Now follows the mantra for Aśvārūḍhā: "Oṃ ehi parameśvari svāhā. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this ten-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Virāj meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Aśvārūḍhā, on the heart. Then, having declared the application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one says with palms joined: "Oṃ ehi hṛdayā..."

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) thus: *Oṃ namaḥ parameśvari śirase svāhā*, *Oṃ svāhā śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Oṃ ehi kavacāya huṃ*, *Oṃ parameśvari netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *Oṃ svāhā astrāya phaṭ*, one should perform meditation as follows: "I meditate upon her who is mounted on a horse, endowed with nine powers, possessing an eye in her forehead, and holding with her [left] hand a horsewhip bound with a noose, bringing the victim—who is overwhelmed by passion—to the horse; who holds in her right hand a raised cane-staff adorned with gold; who has the luster of the *bandhūka* flower; and who is bent by her full breasts."

Having meditated thus, at the end of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs], offer [the merit], and prostrate. This ten-syllable mantra begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), or alternatively, it may begin with Bhuvaneśvarī;

in that case, it becomes eleven syllables. The procedure for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begins with *hrāṃ hrīṃ*, etc. The *ṛṣi*, meditation, and so forth are as before. This is the mantra of Aśvārūḍhā. Now, the mantra of Gaurī:

*hrīṃ gauri rudradayite yogeśvari huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the sixteen-syllable mantra. Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) three times with this mantra, one should place the *ṛṣi* on the head.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Salutation to the *anuṣṭubh* metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Gaurī in the heart," and having stated the application (*viniyoga*) as "for the attainment of my desired goal" while joining the palms in reverence, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with *hāṃ hrīṃ*, etc., and meditate: "One should always remember Gaurī, golden-hued, adorned with all ornaments, holding in her two hands a mirror and collyrium as tools, and a noose and a goad. Having meditated thus—placing the first [syllable] on the left and right upper arms, and the others on the left and right lower arms—one should perform the six-limbed ritual for the hands at the end of the recitation (*japa*), offer it, and prostrate.

Now, the mantra of Padmā is: *Hrīṃ padmāvantī svāhā*. Having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with this seven-syllabled mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the goddess Śrī Padmāvatī, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart; salutation to *Śrīṃ*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*), on the private parts; salutation to *Svāhā*, the power (*śakti*), on the feet. The procedure for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begins with *Hrāṃ hrīṃ*, and so forth. The visualization (*dhyāna*): "I meditate upon her who holds a pair of red lotuses in her two hands, who stands upon a lotus, whose seat is a lotus, who has eyes like the Bandhūka flower, who possesses three eyes, and who is radiant with various ornaments."

Having meditated thus, one should perform everything. Now follows the mantra of Jyeṣṭhā Lakṣmī: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ādyalakṣmi svayaṃbhuvam hrīṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. With this seventeen-syllable mantra, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) three times. Then, perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *namaḥ* to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; *namaḥ* to the Aṣṭi meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; *namaḥ* to Jyeṣṭhā Lakṣmī, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart; *śrīṃ* to the seed-syllable (*bīja*), on the private parts; and *hrīṃ* to the power (*śakti*), on the feet. Having performed the placement, extend the hands with the root-vidyā and recite: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *ādyalakṣmi* to the head... [and so forth].

*Rase Svāhā* for the self-born [Jyeṣṭhā], *Śikhāyai Hrīṃ*, *Kavacāya Huṃ*, *Jyeṣṭhāyai Netrāya Namaḥ*, and *Astrāya Phaṭ*—thus performing the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should meditate: "Seated upon a lotus throne, ruddy in hue, wearing ruddy garments, her limbs smeared with saffron powder, her eyes like full-blown lotuses, with a face of gentle smile; Jyeṣṭhā, holding a water-pot (*kalaśa*) and a vessel of wealth (*vasupātraka*) in her two upper arms, as well as a noose (*pāśa*) and a goad (*aṅkuśa*). Having thus meditated, and having visualized [the other goddesses] starting from the left upper [arm] and so on, and those situated below the first and so on, respectively.

Then, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs] upon the vessel (*kalaśa*) filled with nectar, offer it, and prostrate. This is the mantra of Jyeṣṭhā Lakṣmī. Now, the Tripuṭā mantra:

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the three-syllable mantra *Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Saṃmohana Bhṛgu on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī meter on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Tripuṭā on the heart. Having performed this, one should repeat *Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ* twice and perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the individual syllables alone, and then meditate as follows: [She who is] golden-hued...

I meditate upon her who stands upon a beautiful lion-throne in a lotus, situated on a jeweled floor within a golden pavilion in a forest grove of radiant *pārijāta* trees; she rests within a hexagon, holding in her lotus-hands a pair of lotuses, a bow, an arrow, a goad, and a rosary, wearing a crown of jewels and lovely ornaments, possessing three eyes, and surrounded on all sides by auspicious female messengers carrying chowries, mirrors, caskets, boxes, and betel-rolls. Having thus meditated, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other limbs (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*), and offer the recitation.
"One should prostrate"—this is the Tripuṭā mantra.

(Ṭhīṣ FOḻīO īṣ BḻāṇK) Now, the mantra of Śivadūtī: *hrīṃ śivadūtyai namaḥ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this seven-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *namaḥ* to the Seer Rudra on the head; *namaḥ* to the Gāyatrī metre on the mouth; *namaḥ* to the deity Śrī Śivadūtī Nityā on the heart; *namaḥ* to the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* on the private parts; *namaḥ* to the Power (*śakti*) on the feet; and *namaḥ* to Śivadūtī on the navel.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Oṃ namaḥ tyai kīlakāya," and having stated the ritual application (*viniyoga*), one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with *Hrāṃ Hrīm* and so forth, and then meditate [upon her] as follows: She is equal in brilliance to the midday sun, free from the divisions of time; she wears a crown of nine jewels, has three eyes, and is rosy-hued. Her body is adorned with various precious gems and shines with [her] locks of hair. She possesses a pure smile and eight arms, and is being praised by great seers (*maharṣi*).

With her left hands, she holds a noose (*pāśa*), a shield (*kheṭa*), a mace (*gadā*), and a jewel-topped staff (*ratnacchaṭaka*); with her right hands, she likewise holds a goad (*aṅkuśa*), a sword (*khaḍga*), an axe (*kuṭhāra*), and a lotus (*kamala*), bestowing boons upon the practitioner.

Having meditated thus: "Endowed with the six gestures (ṣaṭ-dāna) and the eightfold form," and having performed the *japa* at its conclusion, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other limbs, offer the *japa*, and perform the obeisance (*praṇāma*). This is the mantra of the Nityā Śivadūtī. Now, the mantra of the Nityā Tvaritā: *Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ khecachekṣa strī huṃ kṣe hrīṃ phaṭ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twelve-syllable mantra, one should assign the limbs as follows: "Salutation to the sage Arjuna on the head; salutation to the Virāṭ meter on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Tvaritā Nityā on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable *ūṃ* on the private parts; salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hrīṃ* on the feet. Thus.

Having performed the assignment (*nyāsa*) with palms joined in reverence and stated the ritual application (*viniyoga*), one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) as follows: *che* to the heart, *kṣe* to the head, *kṣa* to the weapon, *trī* to the crest, *strī* to the armor, *huṃ* to the eye, and *kṣe* phaṭ to the weapon. Then, one should meditate [on the Goddess] whose body shines with the splendor of Śiva, whose lotus-feet are illuminated by a red lotus, and who is radiant with the brilliance of her ornaments—the crown, armlets, girdle, and anklets. She is adorned with eight serpents, each of two-fold gait, representing the four castes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—appearing in their respective forms. Among them, Śeṣa and Vāsuki are the Brahmins, while Tarkṣya and... [the text continues].

The two kings were Karkoṭaka and Padma; the two Vaiśyas were Mahāpadma and Kulika; and the two Śūdras were Śaṅkha and Śaṅkhapāla. She was adorned with beautiful armlets made of *pakṣava* and *kṣakasaṃvīta*, her arms graced by moving ornaments, and she shone with a crown of rubies. Her hair was bound with a crest of peacock feathers, and she bore a parasol topped with banners. Her round breasts gleamed with strings of *guñjā* berries, and she possessed three eyes, a lovely face, and a lotus-like countenance with a joyful smile. Adorned with earrings and a crown, her form was slender, and she held the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her two hands.

The wise practitioner should meditate upon the Goddess Taruṇī, who is the abode of grace, possessing large, uplifted breasts, with the rays of her reddish, elongated eyes, and lips as crimson as young sprouts.

Having thus meditated, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) on the hands, offer the merit, and prostrate. This is the mantra of Tvaritā Nityā. Now, the mantra of Trikaṇṭhikā: having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the three-syllable mantra "Huṃ khe kṣi," one should assign: to Arjuna, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; to Virāṭ, the Metre (*chandas*), in the mouth; and to the deity Śrī Trikaṇṭhikā, in the heart. Thus [it is said].

Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating the mantra twice, one should meditate as follows: One should always contemplate the Goddess who removes fear—she whose lotus-navel shines with the luster of a lotus stalk, whose throat possesses a reddish glow, whose face is radiant, and who has four faces adorned with large earrings. She is terrifying with her bared fangs, holding a conch, a discus, a sword, and a lotus in her hands, and she bears the moon upon her crest. Her forehead-eye is blazing forth. Having meditated thus—with "four" meaning four [faces], "conch" (*dara*) meaning a shell, and "discus" (*ari*) meaning a wheel; with the conch and discus in the left and right upper hands respectively, and the other two weapons in the remaining two hands—one should proceed.

At the end of the recitation according to one's capacity, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣi* and other elements, one should offer the recitation. This is the *Trikaṇṭakī* mantra. Now, the *Vaśya-Trikaṇṭakī* mantra: having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the three-syllable mantra "Khe Strī Kṣe," and having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the doubled syllables of the mantra, one should perform everything else, such as the visualization (*dhyāna*), as previously described. Now, the Vaiṣṇavī mantra:

having performed three breath-controls with the eight-syllable mantra "A Ka Ca Ṭa Ta Pa Ya Śa," [one should place] Nārada as the *ṛṣi* on the head, the *anuṣṭubh* meter in the mouth, and the deity Śrī-Vaiṣṇavī in the heart.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the following applications: *Oṃ a ka ca hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ ka ca ṭa śirase svāhā*, *Oṃ ca ṭa ta śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Oṃ ṭa ta pa kavacāya huṃ*, *Oṃ ta pa na netrebhyo vauṣaṭ*, and *Oṃ pa ya śa astrāya phaṭ*; one should meditate [on the Goddess] as follows: She resembles a red lotus, her hair is loose and flowing, and she is radiant with shimmering golden earrings.

She wears a crown bound with gold and jewels and adorned with a string of pearls. She is beautifully adorned with three eyes—white, black, and reddish-brown—and her teeth, tongue, and girdle are the color of the bandhūka flower. She is Śrī...
She had six radiant nostrils, a curved neck, and large eyes; she possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns. She was four-armed and adorned with a garland, her breasts were full and elevated.

In her upper right hand she held a sword, and in the other a *siddhasūtra*; she bore the *siddhasūtra* as a rosary. With her two left hands she bestowed the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons. With her body she leaned perfectly against a jeweled pillar, her navel deep, her ankles hidden, and her heels well-formed. She repeatedly uttered the words, "What do you desire?", standing before the five-faced one.

Having meditated thus: "Beholding her own vehicle," one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity; at the conclusion of the recitation, having performed the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other limbs (*ṛṣyādi-vinyāsa*), and having offered the merit of the recitation, one should prostrate. This is the mantra of Vaiṣṇavī: *oṃ mahāmāyāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ vaiṣṇavyai namaḥ*.

Regarding these two mantras of Vaiṣṇavī—the eight-syllable and the five-syllable—the *ṛṣi*, meditation, and so forth should be understood as before. Now, the mantra of Vagalāmukhī: *oṃ vāgālāmukhi sarvaduṣṭānāṃ vācaṃ mukhaṃ padaṃ staṃbhaya jihvāṃ kīlaya buddhiṃ vināśaya hrīṃ uṃ svāhā*. By means of this thirty-six-syllable mantra, [one should perform] the vitalization (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*).

Having performed the assignment (*nyāsa*) for three watches (*yāma*), saying: "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; obeisance to Triṣṭubh, the Metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; obeisance to Śrī Vagalāmukhī, the Deity (*devatā*), on the heart; obeisance to *hlīṃ*, the Seed-syllable (*bīja*), on the private parts; obeisance to *svāhā*, the Power (*śakti*), on the feet"; and having declared the application (*viniyoga*) with palms joined: *oṃ hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* (obeisance to the heart); *vagalāmukhi śirase svāhā* (Vagalāmukhi, obeisance to the head, *svāhā*); *sarvaduṣṭānāṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (of all the wicked, obeisance to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*); *vācamukhaṃ padaṃ staṃbhaya kavacāya huṃ* (paralyze speech, mouth, and step; obeisance to the armor, *huṃ*); *jihvāṃ kīlaya netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ* (pin the tongue; obeisance to the two eyes, *vauṣaṭ*); *buddhiṃ vināśaya astrāya phaṭ* (destroy the intellect; obeisance to the weapon, *phaṭ*).

Having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantra "strāyaphaṭ" at the heart and other locations, one should meditate [upon her] as follows: She is profound and greatly intoxicated, resembling molten gold, four-armed, and three-eyed, seated upon a lotus throne. In her right hands she holds a mallet and a noose; in her left hands, a tongue and a vajra. She wears yellow garments, possesses thick, firm, and full breasts, and is adorned with golden earrings. She has a yellow crescent moon as her crest-jewel, is decorated with yellow ornaments, and is seated upon a golden lion-throne. Her right lower and upper hands hold the mallet and noose, while her left lower and upper hands hold the tongue and vajra.

Having meditated thus: "The Vajra-speech [is for] the person who is an adversary to the practitioner," one should perform the recitation according to one's capacity; at the end of the recitation, having performed the placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, one should offer the recitation to the Goddess and prostrate.

This is the mantra of Vagalamukhī. Now, the mantra of Chinnamastā: *Śrīṃ hrīṃ huṃ aiṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this sixteen-syllable mantra, or alternatively, having performed three breath-controls with the thirteen-syllable mantra: *Oṃ vajraṃ vairocanīye huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should place the seer upon the head... [at the wound].

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Oṃ *namaḥ* to the face, to the *Saṃrāṭ* metre; Oṃ *namaḥ* to the heart, to the deity Chinnamastaka," one should place [the mantras] with the two thumbs and the two little fingers, saying: "Oṃ Āṃ, *namaḥ* to the sword, to the heart. One should place [the mantra] with the two index fingers and the two ring fingers, saying: "Oṃ Iṃ, *svāhā* to the beautiful sword, to the head. One should place [the mantra] with the two middle fingers and on the two middle fingers themselves, saying: "Oṃ Ūṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to the glorious thunderbolt, to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*). One should place [the mantra] with the two ring fingers and the two index fingers, saying: "Oṃ Aiṃ, *huṃ* to the noose, to the armor (*kavaca*). Oṃ Ā Ī I U Ū...

One should place [the seed-syllables] with the mantra *ṛ ḷ ḷ e ai o au aṃ aḥ asura yakṣa phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ astrāya phaṭ* upon the two thumbs using the two little fingers; in this manner, one should assign them to the five limbs beginning with the heart, excluding the eyes. Now, for the meditation (*dhyāna*): it is threefold—*sakala* (with parts), *niṣkala* (without parts), and *kalātīta* (beyond parts). Regarding the *sakala* form: one should meditate on a lotus in one's own navel, white and fully blossomed through faith. In the center of that lotus-bud is the orb of the fierce-rayed sun, resembling the *japā* flower and like the red *bandhūka*. It is the circle of the source (*yonimaṇḍala*), consisting of the lines of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*.

In the midst of that [fire] was that Goddess, blazing with a splendor equal to ten million suns; she held her own head, severed by a sword, in her hand; she had a wide-open mouth and was terrifying, licking her tongue and drinking the stream of blood arising from her own beloved; her mass of hair was disheveled and adorned with various flowers; she wore a garland of heads in her right hand, was naked, possessed a magnificent form, stood in the pratyālīḍha posture, bore a necklace of bones, and had a serpent as her sacred thread; she appeared to be sixteen years of age.

Some practitioners meditate on her who has two full, lofty breasts and is seated upon Rati and Kāma; others should meditate on Rati and Manobhava engaged in inverted intercourse. One should meditate on Varṇinī joined with Ḍākinī at the left and right sides. One should meditate on Ḍākinī situated on the right side, while on the left side is Varṇinī—red in color, gentle, with loose hair, naked, holding a skull-cup and a flaying-knife in her left and right hands respectively, and drinking the stream of blood flowing from the Goddess’s neck, wearing a garland of bones.

I bow to the Great Goddess, who has a *nāga* as her sacred thread; who is a *ḍākinī* on her left side, resembling a cloud at the end of an aeon; whose eyes flash like streaks of lightning; whose rows of teeth belong to *talākinīs*; whose face is terrifying with its fangs; who possesses two full and high breasts; who has loose hair, is most formidable, and is naked; whose great tongue lolls out; who is adorned with a garland of severed heads;

who holds a skull-cup and a flaying knife in her right and left hands respectively; and who is drinking the stream of blood flowing from the neck of the Goddess, appearing fearsome with the human skull in her hand.

The wise practitioner should meditate upon that most terrifying Goddess being attended by these two. She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; the meaning is that she stands with her two feet drawn together with the intent of restraining the intense pressure arising from the source of Rati and Kāma. Now, for the meditation on the formless (*niṣkala*): One should contemplate the Great Goddess in the center of one's own navel, which is like a pure lotus adorned by the orb of the sun, joined with the wheel of the womb (*yonicakra*), and endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*). There, in the middle, one should think of her as having a subtle form, shaped like the flame of a lamp, established in non-duality. Ka...

One should meditate upon her who is joined with the *rakacchapikā* posture, seated in the *baddha-padmāsana*, endowed with the *yonimudrā*, with her eyes fixed on the heart, and possessing a pair of full breasts; this meditation is known as the "partless" (*niṣkala*) and is to be meditated upon by householders. Now, as for the meditation on *Kalāvatī* to be meditated upon by ascetics: within the interior of one's own body, at the navel-lotus, she is found—untainted, beyond qualities, gentle, like the luster of the crescent moon, accessible through concentration alone, encircled by the three qualities, yet transcending parts and transcending the qualities, [the state of] liberation.

Having thus meditated upon her as the bestower of the path, one should perform recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity; at its conclusion, having performed the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other factors (*ṛṣyādi-vinyāsa*) and offered the oblation, one should prostrate. This is the *Chinnamastā-mantra*. [Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Mantracandrikā* composed by Svāmī Janārdana Bhaṭṭa. Now, for the *Ugratārā-mantra*: *hrīṃ trīṃ huṃ phaṭ oṃ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this five-syllabled mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows:

"Obeisance to Brahmā, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; obeisance to the *Gāyatrī* metre on the mouth; obeisance to the deity Śrī Ugratārā in the heart; obeisance to the seed-syllable *huṃ* in the private parts."

Having thus performed the placement [of the syllables] and having applied the six limbs with *hrāṃ hrīṃ* and so forth, one should meditate [on her] as follows: Born from the seed-syllable *Huṃ*, she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, trampling a corpse with her feet; she laughs a terrible, loud *aṭṭahāsa*; she holds a sword, a blue lotus, and a *kartṛ* (scimitar) in her short arms. She arises from the seed-syllable *Huṃ*. She is short, her matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*) are dark blue, massive, and tawny, and she is encircled by fierce serpents. Having cast away dullness, she destroys the inertia of the worlds; she is Ugratārā herself, holding a skull-staff (*kapālakhaṭvāṅga*). With the intent of crushing the hearts of corpses with her *pratyālīḍha* stance, her feet are drawn together, and from her upper right hand... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available text.)

Having meditated on the weapon (*āyudha*) as "rādyetadādivāmayoranye" and so forth, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other limbs (*ṛṣyādika-vinyāsa*), offer the recitation to the Goddess, and prostrate. This is the mantra of Ugratārā. Now, the mantra of Dakṣiṇakālī: *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ dakṣiṇekālike krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-two-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement of the limbs: "Salutation to Bhairava, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to the *triṣṭubh* meter on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā on the heart."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Obeisance to the Deity" at the heart; "Obeisance to the secret *huṃ* seed-syllable" at the private parts; and "Obeisance to the power (*śakti*) *hrīṃ*" at the feet; and having declared with palms joined, "This is the application for the sake of attaining my desired goal," one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the six long vowels beginning with *krāṃ krīṃ*, etc., and then meditate: [One should meditate on] the divine Kālikā of the South, whose face is terrifying, who has disheveled hair and four arms, adorned with a garland of severed heads, holding a sword and a freshly severed head in her left hands, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons in her right hands.
With her hands hanging down and up, possessing a great luster like fat, dark-complexioned, and likewise naked; smeared with blood dripping from the mass of matted hair clinging to her neck;

adorned with two corpses brought to serve as her ear-ornaments; her face made terrifying by formidable fangs, with full and elevated breasts; having fashioned a girdle from multitudes of corpses; snatching away [souls] with her mouth; her face quivering with streams of blood flowing from both corners of her lips; of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, dwelling in the cremation ground, protruding teeth, and with long, loose locks spreading to the right—[he beheld her].

One should thus contemplate Kālī, who dwells in the cremation ground, seated upon the heart of Mahādeva whose form is the gathering of *vaka* flowers; who is surrounded on the four sides by those whose forms are the malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) of Śivā; who is joined with Mahākāla; who is endowed with the love of the breast of Śavara; whose face is serene and happy, her lotus-like countenance smiling. Having meditated thus, having performed the recitation (*japa*), and having assigned the *ṛṣi* and other limbs, one should offer the recitation to the Goddess and bow to the deity and the Guru. This is the mantra of Dakṣiṇakālī. Now, the mantra of Dhūmavatī: *dhūṃ dhūṃ dhūmā*.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the eight-syllable mantra *mārvātī svāhā*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Pippalāda Ṛṣi" on the head; "Salutation to Nivṛt Chandas" on the mouth; and "Salutation to the deity Śrī Dhūmāvatī" on the heart. Then, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands, heart, and other parts using the syllables *dhāṃ* and *dhīm* (and so forth), one should meditate as follows: "She is pale in complexion, of restless form, dark, tall, and clad in soiled garments. Her hair is disheveled and coarse, she is a widow, and her teeth are sparse. She is mounted upon a crow-bannered vehicle and carries a dangling water-pot."

Having meditated thus: "Dharā has hands as harsh as the rays of the sun; she is swift with hands that shake like milk; her body is covered in thick hair and she is matted-haired; her eyes are crooked; she is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, and is always intent on impurity"—one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability, assign the *ṛṣi* and other limbs [of the mantra], offer the recitation to the Goddess, and prostrate. This is the mantra of Dhūmāvatī. Now, the mantra of Bhadrakālī: *Hauṃ kāli mahākāli kiṇi kiṇi phaṭ svāhā*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this fourteen-syllable mantra, [one should proceed].

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by placing [the mantras] upon the heart and other parts—namely: *Ṛṣyādikamasya* (for the ṛṣi, etc.), *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *kāli śirase svāhā*, *mahākāli śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *kiṇikiṇika kavacāya huṃ phaṭ*, *netrāya vauṣaṭ*, and *astrāya phaṭ*—one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: "I am she who, emaciated by hunger, with hollow eyes and a face soiled with impurities, with disheveled hair and bared fangs, having become satiated, now makes this entire world her single morsel of food. With my two hands, I hold a fierce noose resembling the flames of a blazing fire, and with my teeth..."

Having meditated thus—“May Bhadrakālī, who resembles the fruit of the Jambū tree, protect me from both [fear] and bestow auspiciousness”—one should perform the recitation (*japa*), execute the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), offer the recitation, and prostrate.

This is the mantra of Bhadrakālī. Now, the mantra of Mahākālī: *Oṃ śe śe ṅkre ṅkre paśuṃ gṛhāṇa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having performed three breath-retentions (*prāṇāyāma*) with this fourteen-syllable mantra, and having performed the purifications through ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the [assignment of] seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth—there being no further deliberation required here—the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows: [One should meditate on her] as five-faced, extremely fierce, with three eyes in each face...

Having meditated upon the Goddess as holding in her right and left hands a spear, a trident, a bow, arrows, a shield, a sword, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, and adorned with serpent ornaments—one should offer the recitation (*japa*) and prostrate.

Now, the mantra of Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī: *Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī Sumukhī Mahāpiśācinī Hrīṃ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-two-syllable mantra, one should meditate [on her]. There is no [prescribed] seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth. As follows: seated upon a corpse, red in color...

The best of mantra-knowers should meditate upon her with the left and right hands joined: she is adorned with fine garments, endowed with red ornaments, and resplendent with a necklace of *guñjā* seeds; she is sixteen years old and red in complexion, possessing full, high, and firm breasts; she holds a skull-cup and a curved knife (*kartṛkā*) in her pair of hands, and is the embodiment of light. Having offered an oblation (*bali*) with the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*), one should recite [the mantra] with the mind fixed upon her. One who desires success must perform the recitation only with the remnants; all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arise from the rosary of recitation performed with the remnants. Then, having offered the recitation, one should prostrate. Now...

The mantra of Siṃhavaktrā: *Hrīṃ mahāyogini gauri bhayaṅkarī huṃ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this sixteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Aṅgiras on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Mahākṛtyā in the heart. Having stated the application (*viniyoga*), [one recites]: *Hrāṃ hrāṃ mahāyogini gauri huṃ phaṭ*—salutation to the heart; *Hrīṃ hrīṃ bhuvanabhayaṅkari huṃ phaṭ*—[salutation] to the head; *Hrīṃ hrīṃ mahāyogini gauri*... [and so forth].

Having first performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with: *phaṭ* for the crest (*śikhā*), *hrauṃ hrīṃ bhuvanabhayaṃkarī huṃ phaṭ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *hrauḥ hrīṃ mahāyoginī gauri phaṭ* for the eyes (*netra*), and *hraḥ hrīṃ bhuvanabhayaṃkarī phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*), one should meditate as follows: She is seated upon a lion-throne, black-faced, with breasts hanging down, her face formidable with fangs, three-eyed, and blazing on all sides. She is clothed in a black bodice, possesses a luster like smokeless fire, and holds in her lotus-like hands a trident, a discus, a wine-cup (*caṣaka*), and a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*).

Having meditated thus: "She who has a great tongue constantly lolling out, terrifying with eyes like lightning," and having performed the recitation (*japa*), assigned the *ṛṣi* and other limbs (*nyāsa*), and offered [the merit], one should prostrate. This is the mantra of Mahākṛtyā. Now, the mantra of Dhanadāyakṣiṇī: *Raṃ hnīṃ śrīṃ ratipriye svāhā*. Having restrained the breath three times with this nine-syllable mantra, one should meditate.

There is no requirement for the assignment of limbs (*nyāsakalpanā*) here. As follows: "In the midst of a golden enclosure, seated upon a golden yellow throne, a young Yakṣī who emits a pervasive fragrance..."

She was burdened by the weight of the monks who shone like gold, endowed with full and lofty breasts, possessing eyes like blue lotuses and a reddish complexion, with trembling red lotuses in her hands and wearing no fine garments.

Having meditated thus on the hosts of limbs adorned with red [garments and ornaments], and having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, one should offer it with the mantra "O secret, most secret... and prostrate. Now, for the *Śītalā* mantra: With the nine-syllable mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śītalāyai Namaḥ," one should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then, one should assign the parts of the mantra: "Salutation to Upamanyu, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), to the head"; "Salutation to the Bṛhatī meter, to the mouth"; "Salutation to the deity Śrī Śītalā, to the heart. Then: "Hrāṃ Śrāṃ, salutation to the Heart"; "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, Svāhā to the Head"; "Hrūṃ Śrūṃ, Vaṣaṭ to the Tuft of Hair (*śikhā*"); "Hraiṃ Śraiṃ, Hum to the Armor (*kavaca*)."

Having performed the single-syllable six-limbed nyāsa with the mantras *hrauṃ śrauṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ* and *hraḥ śraḥ astrāya phaṭ*, one should meditate [on her] as naked, holding in her two hands a winnowing basket and a broom.

One should meditate upon Śītalā, seated upon a donkey, resembling a dark blue cloud, with red unguents and garments, and adorned with red garlands—thus one should always meditate for the destruction of diseases. Having thus meditated, one should offer the recitation (*japa*) and prostrate. For this mantra, ten thousand recitations (*ayuta*) are required, and the fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that. As for its application: standing in water reaching the navel, one should recite the mantra a thousand times; then even most dreadful diseases such as boils and eruptions will quickly perish. Thus [says] Gosvāmī Janārdana.

In the *Maṃtracandrikā*, the fifth chapter [is concluded]. The section on the Śakti-mantras is finished. Now, regarding the Vaiṣṇava mantras: having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the eight-syllable mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya," one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "To the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Sadhya" at the head; "To the Goddess Gāyatrī" at the mouth; "To the Divine Being, the Supreme Self (Śrī Paramātman)" at the heart. Having stated the application (*viniyoga*), one should assign: "To the Fiery Spark (Kruśolkā), Svāhā! at the heart; "To the Great Spark (Maholkā), Svāhā! at the head; "To the Heroic Spark (Vīrolkā), Svāhā! at the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

Having performed the assignment of the five limbs (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*)—namely, "To the fire-brand body, Svāhā," "To the thousand-fold fire-brand, Svāhā," and "To the weapon, Phaṭ"—upon the little finger, thumb, heart, and so forth, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows: I worship in my heart the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, clad in yellow garments, bearing in his [right] hands the discus, conch, mace, and lotus; possessing the splendor of the sun's orb; with his radiant sides adorned by the illustrious Earth; wearing a crown, marked with the Śrīvatsa, possessing the Kaustubha gem and a great necklace, shining with armlets and necklaces, adorned with glittering earrings, and holding the conch and other weapons in his lower left hands.

Having meditated that "the first two [syllables] are at the beginning" and "the others are above," and having performed the *japa*, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other limbs at the end of the recitation: "O you, the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this *japa* performed by me; may success be mine, O God, through your grace, for you abide within me. Having thus offered the *japa* and prostrated, this is the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa. Alternatively, there is the Vāsudeva mantra: "oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twelve-syllabled mantra, one should assign: "Salutation to Prajāpati, the seer (*ṛṣi*), upon the head; to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), upon the mouth."

"OṂ CHANDESE NAMAḤ" [at the heart]; "ŚRĪVĀSUDEVĀYA DEVATĀYAI NAMAḤ" [at the head]. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should say: "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of all my desired goals. With palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) on both hands with the root mantra, one should place the five limb-mantras on the hands from the thumb to the little finger—excluding the eyes—as follows: "OṂ HṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ" [at the heart]; "NAMAḤ ŚIRASE SVĀHĀ" [at the head]; "BHAGAVATE ŚIKHĀYAIVAṢAṬ" [at the crest-lock]; "VĀSUDEVĀYA KAVACĀYA HUṂ" [at the armor]; "OṂ NAMO BHAGAVATE VĀSUDEVĀYA ASTRĀYA PHAṬ" [at the weapon]. [Thus one should perform the placement of the five limbs, excluding the eyes.]

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) from the heart to the weapon-mantra, one should perform meditation as follows: In the center of an ocean of milk, upon an island inhabited by celestial women, one should contemplate a forest frequented by all the seasons.

In its midst stands a divine Kalpa tree of wondrous appearance; beneath it is a single jewel-throne of pure luster, resplendent with a mass of light like the shining full moon of autumn. Therein, one should contemplate the god Vāsudeva, whose face is graced with a smile, and whose hands hold a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus.

He who deludes the three worlds with a splendor as radiant as ten thousand moons; whose staff-like arms shine with armlets and bracelets and are adorned with jewels; who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and a crown of excellent gems, and is marked by the Kaustubha;

whose long eyes are beautiful and copper-red like the petals of a lotus, and whose cheeks are illuminated by shimmering earrings; who wears yellow garments and a neck adorned with necklaces and garlands;

whose throat is graced by beautiful bracelets, and whose broad chest shines with a blossoming forest garland; [he whom] Sanaka and other lords of sages approached, desiring a determination of the ultimate truth.

Having meditated upon the visualization of the weapons beginning from the upper left hand and ending with the lower right hand—[the deity] who is served by hosts of *ādityas*, *diti-jas* (demons), and *gandharvas*, and attended by *siddhas*, *vidyādharas*, and great serpents (*mahoragas*)—one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity. At the conclusion of the recitation, having assigned the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs], and having offered the recitation to the Deity, one should prostrate. This is the Vāsudeva mantra.
Now, the Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ lakṣmīvāsudevāya namaḥ*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this fourteen-syllable mantra, [one should proceed].

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to Prajāpati, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the face; salutation to the deity Śrī Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva on the heart," and having joined the palms in reverence, saying, "For the attainment of all my desires, [I offer] *viyogi*," one should recite the five-limbed mantras: *Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ śirase svāhā*; *Oṃ lakṣmī śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *Oṃ vāsudevāya kavacāya huṃ*; *Oṃ namaḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Then, with the hands touched by the root mantra, [one should perform the placement] upon the fingers...

Having placed [the syllables] on the limbs according to the *liṣu* (the sequence of six), and having placed them on the heart and other centers excluding the eyes and the arrows, one should meditate as follows: May He grant prosperity—He whose body is beautiful like the rising lightning and the moon, adorned with ornaments, and who, out of a desire for perfect union with the lotus-eyed Śrī, appears as if their forms have become one; He who holds a mirror with a lotus and a jeweled pitcher in His uplifted left hands, and a divine lotus, mace, conch, and discus in His right hands positioned from top to bottom. (Note: "Left" and "right" here refer to the deity's perspective; the mirror, lotus, and pitcher are in the upper left hands, while the lotus, mace, conch, and discus are in the upper right hands.)

Having meditated that the four objects of meditation are the lotus and so forth, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other limbs, offer the recitation to the deity, and prostrate.

This is the procedure for the Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva mantra. Now, the mantra consisting of Hari and Hara: *Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ śaṅkaranārāyaṇāya namaḥ hrauṃ hrīṃ oṃ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this sixteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the limb-placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to the *anuṣṭubh* meter on the mouth; [salutation] to Śrī Hari-Hara on the heart."

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Obeisance to Yadevatā" and declared the application (*viniyoga*) as "for the attainment of all my desired goals" with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using *hrāṃ hrīṃ* and so forth, and then perform meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: "I worship Hari-Hara, who holds a trident, a discus, the Pāñcajanya conch, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, whose body is half-blue according to his own nature. This is the meditation on the weapons, starting from the upper right hand and ending with the lower left. Having meditated thus, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) as much as possible. At the end of the recitation, having placed the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other components [of the mantra], one should offer the recitation to the deity.

Having offered this and prostrated, [this is] the *itihariharamantra*. Now follows the *dadhi-vāmana-mantra*: "Oṃ namo viṣṇave surāṃpataye mahābalāya svāhā. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this eighteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Indu in the head; salutation to the Virāj meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Dadhivāmana in the heart. Then, with palms joined, one declares: "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation (*japa*) for the attainment of all my desired goals. [Then: "Oṃ, salutation to the heart."

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by assigning the mantras—*namaḥ śirase svāhā*, *viṣṇave śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *surāṃpataye kavacāya huṃ*, *mahābalāya netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ svāhā*, and *astrāya phaṭ*—to the two hands from the thumbs to the palms, and having likewise assigned them to the six limbs starting with the heart, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: [He who is] seated upon a white lotus beneath a parasol of nectar-jewels, shining like the full moon; whose sides are embraced by Śrī and Bhūmi; who resembles a crystal gem and is adorned with every variety of ornament; [and who holds] in his left hand...
May Viṣṇu, known as the illustrious Vāmana, who bestows desired objects and constantly holds a golden cup filled with nectar and a pitcher of divine ambrosia, protect you both.

Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability, and having assigned the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā* at the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer the recitation to the God and prostrate. This is the *Dadhivāmana-mantra*.
Now, the *Yajñeśvara-mantra*: *Oṃ klīṃ śrīṃ vaṃ oṃ namo viṣṇave surāṃpataye mahābalāya svāhā*. With this twenty-two-syllable mantra, [one should perform] the *prāṇāyāma*.

Having performed the assignment [of mantras] for three watches (*yāma*)—assigning "Obeisance to the Sage Cyavana" to the head, "Obeisance to the *Gāyatrī* metre" to the mouth, and "Obeisance to the deity Śrī-Yajñeśvara-Vāmana" to the heart—and having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with "klāṃ klīṃ m" and so forth, one should meditate as follows: "The God, white as camphor, seated upon a divine lotus, with a gracious countenance and beautiful eyes, enchanting with a lovely smile; holding a staff and a jar of nectar, possessing a luster equal to the autumnal moon, and carrying a fine vessel of curd-rice with side-dishes."

One should meditate upon Hari, the primordial of the worlds and the remover of the world's suffering. Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other factors, offer the recitation, and prostrate.

This is the mantra of Vāmana, the Lord of Sacrifice. Now, the mantra of Bhogavāmana: "Oṃ namo bhagavate viṣṇave surāṃpataye mahābalāya svāhā. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-two-syllable mantra, one should assign: "Salutation to the sage Kapila on the head; to the Gāyatrī metre on the mouth..."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Oṃ *maḥ*! Homage to the deity who bestows enjoyment upon the heart," and having declared the application (*viniyoga*) as "for the attainment of desired success" while joining the palms in reverence, one should recite: "Oṃ *namaḥ*! To the Blessed One—*hṛt*; to Viṣṇu—*śiras*; to the one who strikes down demons—*śikhā*; to the one of great power—*kavaca*; *svāhā* to the eyes—*netra*; *astram*. Having thus applied these six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*) from the thumbs to the palms of both hands, and having also applied them to the six limbs starting from the heart, one should meditate on Vāmana, the Lord of Sacrifice, white as camphor, and having performed the recitation (*japa*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and so forth for the *japāteḥ* mantra, one should offer the recitation (*japa*). Thus ends the *Bhogavāmana* mantra. Now follows the *Māyāvālakavāmana* mantra: *oṃ namo māyāvālakaviṣṇave surāṃpataye mahābalāya svāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-three-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement as follows:

"Salutation to Brahmā, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the *chandas*, on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Māyāvālakavāmana on the heart. Having thus performed the placement, [one should proceed] for the sake of [attaining] desires...

Having performed the application (*viniyoga*) for the sake of the accomplishment of all goals, one should speak with palms joined in reverence: "Oṃ namo hṛdayāya māyāvālaka śiraḥ viṣṇave śikhā surāṃ mataye kavacaṃ mahābalāya netraṃ svāhā astram. Having thus assigned the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*) from the thumbs to the little fingers of both hands, and having likewise assigned them to the six limbs beginning with the heart, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: "Hari, wearing yellow lower and upper garments, gentle, holding a girdle and a loincloth, bearing a water-pot, a staff, and an umbrella in his hands..."

Having meditated thus: "The one wearing a sacred thread (*jñopavītī*), dark-blue like a cloud, the deceptive dwarf (*rachadmavāmana*) should be meditated upon," and having performed the *nyāsa* of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and others at the end of the recitation, one should offer the recitation and prostrate.

This is the *māyāvālaka* mantra. Now, for the *hayagrīva* mantra: Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the single-syllable mantra *kṣsrūṃ*, one should perform the *nyāsa*: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Hayagrīva, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart. Then, one should state: "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of desired success. Thus it is done.
