With palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should recite the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*): *hṛt hsīṃ*, *śiraḥ hsrūṃ*, *śikhā hsraiṃ*, *kavacaṃ hsauṃ*, *netraṃ hsaḥ*, and *astrāya phaṭ*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of these mantras on the two hands from the thumbs to the palms, and likewise having performed the placement on the heart and other limbs, one should meditate as follows: "I bow to that Viṣṇu who has the face of a horse, who rests upon a white lotus, whose slender arms at their tips hold a rosary, a lotus, a book, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who is beautiful with a multitude of pure garments and ornaments."

Having meditated on the visualization of the weapons starting from the upper right [hand] down to the lower left, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity. At the conclusion of the recitation, having assigned the *ṛṣi* and other components, one should offer the recitation to the Deity and prostrate. Some state the mantra as "Oṃ Hrayauṃ," while others state it as "Hsraiṃ. In this matter, the recitation and other rites should be performed according to the specific oral instruction. This concludes the Hayagrīva mantra. Now, the second Hayagrīva mantra: Oṃ udgirat praṇavodgītha sarvavāgīśvareśvara sarvavedamaya-aciṃ...

Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the thirty-six-syllable mantra: *tyasarvaṃbodhayabodhayasvāhāhsam*, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the Ṛṣi, on the head; salutation to Anuṣṭubh, the metre, on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Hayagrīva, the deity, on the heart," [one should then recite]: "Oṃ, salutation to the Heart; *udgirat praṇavodgītha*, svāhā to the Head; *sarvavāgīśvareśvara*, vaṣaṭ to the Tuft (*śikhā*); *sarvavedamayācintya*, huṃ to the Armour (*kavaca*); *sarvaṃ bodhaya bodhaya svāhā hsūṃ*, to the Weapon (*astra*)."

Having applied the five-limbed mantras beginning with *phaṭ* to the fingers of the hands consecrated by the root mantra, and having applied them to the heart and other centers—excluding the eyes—one should perform meditation as follows: "I worship Hayagrīva, who has four arms, who is the color of an autumnal cloud, who holds a conch and a discus in his hands, whose face is that of a horse, and whose hand is placed upon a living being. Having meditated thus, performing the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, and at the conclusion of the recitation having assigned the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other components, one should offer the recitation and prostrate. This is the second Hayagrīva mantra.

Now, the third Hayagrīva mantra: *Haṃsaḥ ṛgyajuḥsāmarūpāya vedābharaṇakarmaṇe praṇavodgīthavapuṣe mahāśvaśirase namaḥ so'ham*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this thirty-six-syllable mantra, and having completed the visualization of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other preliminary rites as was done for the previously mentioned thirty-six-syllable mantra, one should conclude. This is the third Hayagrīva mantra. Now, the fourth Hayagrīva mantra: *Haṃsaḥ viśvotīrṇasvarūpāya cinmayā*... [text continues].

"Obeisance to you, Naṃdūrūpin; obeisance to Hayagrīva, the King of Mantras, to Viṣṇu, Svāhā! So am I. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this thirty-eight-syllable mantra, one should perform everything else as prescribed for the previously mentioned thirty-six-syllable mantra. This is the fourth Hayagrīva mantra. Now, the fifth Hayagrīva mantra: "Hsaṃ Hayagrīvāya namaḥ.

Having performed three rounds of breath control with this eight-syllable mantra, one should place [the mantras] on the head: "Obeisance to Brahmā, the Seer (*ṛṣi*); on the mouth: obeisance to the Anuṣṭubh meter (*chaṃdas*); on the heart..."

"Obeisance to the deity Śrīvarāha, the Lord of the Day. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one says with palms joined in reverence: "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation (*japa*) for the attainment of all my desired goals. Then, having touched the two hands with the root mantra, one performs the five-limbed mantras (*pañcāṅga-mantra*) as follows: "Obeisance to the Heart, O One-Horned One (*ekaśṛṅga*). "Svāhā to the Head, O You who are beyond the sky (*vyomātīta*). "Vaṣaṭ to the Tuft (*śikhā*), O Lord of Splendor (*tejodhipati*). "Huṃ to the Armor (*kavaca*), O You of Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*). "Phaṭ to the Weapon (*astra*), O You of Great Tusk (*mahādaṃṣṭra*). Having thus placed these mantras on the fingers from the thumb to the little finger of both hands, one likewise places them on the five limbs excluding the eyes.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should meditate [on the Lord] as follows: from the knees to the feet, he is like refined gold; from the navel to the knees, he is white as the moon; from the neck upwards, he has the brilliance of fire; and from the head to the neck, he is like the moon.

From the site of his crown, he is as beautiful as the sky and possesses a charming splendor. He holds in his excellent hands the discus, conch, sword, shield, mace, spear, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. Adorned with a tusk that supports the entire earth, one should incessantly worship this primordial deity, Varāha, who stands upon the first of the [lotuses] located at the beginning of the right and left [arms].

Some say that [the visualization] is for those situated at the beginning of this [earth element] and others, while others say it is for those situated below the beginning of that [water element] and the rest; thus is the meditation on the Intermediate Dhyāna (Dhyānāntara). One should meditate upon the body of the Earth-bearer (Viṣṇu) as resembling a dark blue cloud, encircled by rising arms, and holding the earth with his white tusks. One should meditate upon the Pārthiva-maṇḍala as having the luster of gold, and the Vāruṇa-maṇḍala as resembling snow. Then, in the fire-element, one should meditate on the fire-like [maṇḍala], and in the air-element, the black [maṇḍala]. In the ether, it should have the luster of lightning; in this way one should meditate upon the Boar. Furthermore, one should meditate upon nectar within the tusk, along with the mountains, forests, and groves.

One should meditate on the wind in the *gī* and the breath in the *huṃ*; likewise, one should meditate on the Moon and Sun in the left and right arms, and the Vasus within the stomach. One should meditate on Brahmā at the feet, Hari in the heart, and Śaṅkara in the mouth. Having thus meditated and performed the victory (*jaya*) according to one's capacity, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other limbs at the conclusion of the recitation, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the Varāha-mantra. Now, the second Varāha-mantra: having performed *prāṇāyāma* with the single-syllable mantra *Huṃ*, [one should assign it] to the head...

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) thus: "Obeisance to Hayagrīva, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), at the mouth; obeisance to Anuṣṭubh, the metre (*chandas*), at the heart; obeisance to Śrī Varāha, the deity (*devatā*), at the heart," and having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with *hāṃ hīṃ huṃ* and so forth, one should meditate as before, [visualizing the deity] from the knees down to the feet, and complete all other remaining rites. This is the second Varāha mantra. Now, for the third Varāha mantra: having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the single-syllable mantra *bhūḥ*, one should perform the seer, the six-limbed placement, and so forth, as in the second mantra.

Having performed [the ritual] in this manner, one should conclude it. This is the third Varāha-mantra. Now follows the fourth Varāha-mantra: "Oṃ bhū-varāhāya namaḥ. Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with this eight-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as follows: "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to Jagatī, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī-Varāha, the deity (devatā), on the heart. Then: "Oṃ, salutation to the heart; bhūṃ, svāhā to the head; varāhāya, vaṣaṭ to the tuft (śikhā); namaḥ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca); Oṃ bhū-varāhāya... [and so forth].

Having performed the assignment (*nyāsa*) of the five-limbed mantras—*namaḥ astrāya phaṭ*—upon the hands consecrated by the root mantra, having assigned them to the fingers ending with the little finger, and having likewise assigned them to the heart and other limbs excluding the eyes, one should meditate as follows: "I worship the God Varāha, whose body is dark blue, whose lotus-face is intensely blue, who sits upon a lotus, and who holds the Earth-power (*kṣoṇī-śakti*) on his lap; who, with his noble arms, eternally bears the conch, mace, lotus, and discus; who possesses fierce splendor, is surrounded by the Earth, Lakṣmī, and Rati, and is clad in skin and sword."

Having meditated on the visualization of the weapons starting from the upper left hand up to the upper right hand with radiant splendors, and having performed the *ṛṣi*-nyāsa and others at the end of the recitation, one should offer the recitation as an oblation.

This is the fourth Varāha-mantra. Now follows the mantra known as Dharā-hṛdaya: "Oṃ namo bhagavatyai dhariṇyai dharāṇidharādhare svāhā. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this nineteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the nyāsa: "Salutation to the sage Varāha on the head; salutation to the Nivṛt meter on the mouth; salutation to Śrīdhara on the heart."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Obeisance to the deity Nya," and having stated the application (*viniyoga*) as "for the attainment of desired success" with palms joined, one should recite the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*): "Oṃ namaḥ to the heart, obeisance; Bhagavatī to the head, svāhā; Dharaṇī to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), vaṣaṭ; O bearer of the earth (*dharaṇidharā*) to the armor (*kavaca*), huṃ; O supporter (*dhare*) to the eyes, vauṣaṭ; svāhā to the weapon (*astra*), phaṭ. Having performed the placement on both hands from the thumbs to the palms, and likewise having performed the placement on the six limbs beginning with the heart, one should meditate as follows: "She who holds a pair of blue lotuses and a cluster of rice stalks..."

Having meditated upon her—who is dark-complexioned, slender, well-adorned, seated upon a lotus on the earth, and holding in her left hands from top to bottom the weapons as described—one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity.

At the conclusion of the recitation, having assigned the *ṛṣi* and other components, one should offer the recitation. This is the mantra known as the Heart of the Earth (*Dharā-hṛdaya*). Now, the Sudarśana mantra: *Oṃ sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this seven-syllable mantra, one should assign: "Salutation to the Ṛṣi Ahi-budhnya" at the head, and "to the Anuṣṭubh metre" at the mouth.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra: "Maḥ! Salutation to the deity, the Great Viṣṇu, who is Śrī Sudarśana in my heart," and having declared the application (*viniyoga*) as being for the attainment of one's desired goal with palms joined, he recites:

"Ācakrāya svāhā, salutation to the heart; Vicakrāya svāhā, svāhā to the head; Sucakrāya svāhā, [salutation] to the tuft (*śikhā*); Aicakrāya hūṃ, [salutation] to the armor (*kavaca*); Sañcakrāya svāhā, vauṣaṭ to the eyes; Jvālācakrāya svāhā, phaṭ to the weapon (*astra*). Having thus performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) with these mantras, he performs the meditation (*dhyāna*).

One should meditate upon Hari, known by the name Rathapada, who holds a discus, a conch, a mace, a lotus, a pestle, a bow, a plow, and a goad; who possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns; who illuminates the minds of the world with the rays of light from his own body and his lotus-like hands; and whose face has formidable, terrifying fangs. Regarding the visualization of the weapons: the discus (*rathāṅga*) and the conch (*hara*) are in the two upper right hands; the goad (*sṛṇi*) and the plow (*aṅkuśa*) are in the first pair of lower hands; the other [mace] is in the second pair of lower hands; and the remaining [lotus and bow] are in the third pair of lower hands. Having meditated thus—

Having performed the recitation (*japa*), at its conclusion, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs], offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the *Sudarśana* mantra. Now, the second *Sudarśana* mantra:
*oṃ namo bhagavate mahāsudarśanāya mahācakrāya mahājvālāya mahādīptarūpāya sarvato māṃ rakṣa mahābalāya svāhā*.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this forty-six-syllable mantra, and having performed everything else—the *ṛṣi*, etc.—as was done for the previous mantra, one should conclude. This is the second.

The mantra of Sudarśana; now the Śrīkara mantra: "Uttiṣṭha śrīkara svāhā. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this eight-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Vāmadeva on the head; salutation to the Paṅktichandas on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrīkara on the heart. Then, with palms joined in reverence, one says: "For the attainment of desired success, this is the application (*viniyoga*). "Bhīṣaya bhīṣaya huṃ—salutation to the heart (*hṛdaya*); trāsaya [trāsaya] huṃ—svāhā to the head (*śiras*); pramardaya pramardaya huṃ—to the crest-lock (*śikhā*)."

Having applied the five-limbed mantras—*ṣaṭ pradhvaṃsaya huṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *rakṣaya huṃ*, and *astrāya phaṭ*—to the fingers ending with the little finger, and likewise to the heart and other limbs excluding the eyes, one should perform the visualization as follows: One should contemplate a white, auspicious island (*śvetadvīpa*) amidst the ocean of milk, which is like a lamp in the midst of a sea of milk that is foaming with a mass of restless waves and garlanded with surging billows. This auspicious island is composed of white [gold], a golden ground strewn with various clusters of jewels, and a grove frequented by all the seasons. One should meditate upon it there.

Where the celestial beings (apsaras) take delight with the gods in that supreme place where the heat is warded off by groves of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma), which resound with the sweet humming of swarms of bees and possess trembling foliage; where it is filled with a frost-like spray from the pollen of clusters of flowers; where the restless swarm of Lakṣmī moves among the golden trees with their jewel-like blossoms, possessing the luster of the beloved of Śakra who is ever-moving; [and] where [the inhabitants] are endowed with nobility, sovereignty, and good fortune, and with youthful forms that are charming and sweet in appearance. I am intoxicated.

With faces illuminated by the moonlight of their palms, their eyes shimmering with the intoxicating luster of the moon-like Jina, they are delightful; they are constantly surrounded by flocks of gods including chatterers and male cuckoos, whose passion is aroused;
they are languid from the weight of their jar-like full breasts; these excellent women move very slowly due to the burden of their beautiful hips.
Such are the Apsarases who sport there with chowries, like the camp of Māra’s general, as if it were the home of the forest-deer or the birthplace of the seasons—a Kalpa-tree one should remember.

He was seated upon the king of birds, whose fame for valor is well-known, who is as radiant as the rising sun, and who rests upon a white lotus; [the bird] whose beautiful golden floor is adorned with great jewels, whose auspicious surface is cool and illuminated by rows of crests, and which is made of the nine precious gems of the brother of Indirā.

He was like molten, pure gold, adorned with beautiful earrings in the shape of makaras from which jewels were emerging, and his crown-jewels illuminated the entire circle of the quarters. His form was lovely.
Her forehead was adorned with a beautiful, pure, and spotless tilaka as white as a crescent moon; her cheeks were radiant like mirrors with their exceedingly flickering earrings;

her face was graced by a smile, shining upon the broad planes of her cheeks; her auspicious lower lip was beautified by a row of teeth and shone like the petal of a ripe bimba fruit or a red lotus leaf;

her eyes were large and beautifully adorned with perfectly applied collyrium; her neck gleamed with the radiance of a multitude of gems from her great necklace; and she bore stalk-like arms illuminated by divine jeweled armlets.

[He saw] Hari, who holds the mace, lotus, conch, and discus with his staff-like arms; who shines brilliantly with a chest that is as broad as a door-panel, the abode of Kamalā, illuminated by the glowing Kaustubha gem, and which serves as the dwelling place for the three worlds; who is resplendent with an abdomen adorned with the three folds and a beautiful line of hair radiating luster; who is lovely with the slope of his hips; who is clad in yellow silk garments and a shimmering jeweled girdle; and whose [thighs] are plump and beautiful like autumnal quivers.
Adorned with beautiful ornaments, his two arms—charming like the neck of a peacock—are radiant with splendor; his feet, resembling red lotuses, have their toes surpassing the tortoise;

his palms are marked by the lotus-emblem of the banner, possessing a luster like the blood of a rabbit; he is eternally embraced by Lakṣmī, who sprinkles him with water from her hands, and is ever enveloped by Forgiveness;

he shines with the brilliance of a fresh ruby, all his limbs resplendent with the beauty of youthful vigor; served by the foremost of gods, asuras, and sages, as well as by hosts of apsarases, he is like the orb of the full moon.

One should meditate upon Him as adorned with those [ornaments], resplendent with fly-whisks (*cāmara*) shimmering like lotuses from the hands of celestial damsels, beautifully graced by victory banners (*vaijayantī*) swaying like streaks of lightning, attended by hosts of Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and Apsarases; with the *yogapīṭha* (seat of yoga) below the left [hand] and the lotus and so forth above the right, and the conch and discus as weapons—having thus meditated, performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, and at the end of the recitation, having assigned the *ṛṣi* and other components and offered the recitation, one should prostrate. This is the Śrīkara mantra. Now...

The second Śrīkara mantra is: "I take refuge at the feet of the glorious Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the glorious Nārāyaṇa. Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with this twenty-four-syllable mantra, and having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and other factors as previously stated for the mantra, one should perform the five-limbed nyāsa with the mantras: *klāṃ* for the heart, *klīṃ* for the head, *klūṃ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *klaiṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*), and *klaḥ* for the weapon (*astra*). Having placed these on the fingers ending with the little finger, and likewise on the heart and other limbs excluding the eyes, one should then perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) on the previous mantra.

Having performed the prescribed recitation (*japa*), at its conclusion, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other components and offer the recitation. This is the second *Śrīkara-mantra*. Now follows the *Puruṣottama-mantra*:

*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ Klīṃ Namaḥ Puruṣottamāpratirūpa-lakṣmī-nivāsa sakala-jagat-kṣobhaṇa sarva-strī-hṛdaya-vidāraṇa tribhuvana-mano-mādakara surāsura-manuja-suṃdarī-jana-manāṃsi tāpaya (2) dīpaya (2) śoṣaya (2) māraya (2) staṃbhaya (2) drāvaya (2) ākarṣa...*
O Lakṣmī, who causes supreme fortune, bestows all auspiciousness, and grants all desires—by means of the discus, mace, sword, and all arrows, pierce [them];

by means of the noose, bind and bind; by means of the goad, strike! *Turu* (twice)! Why do you stand still? Remain [here] until my desired goal is accomplished! *Klīṃ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ oṃ*.

Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra consisting of two hundred and one syllables, one should offer salutation to the sage Jaimini upon the head: *śirasi jaiminaye ṛṣaye namaḥ*.

"Salutation to Amitāya by means of the *Chandas* (meter) in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Puruṣottama in the heart. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of one's desired goal.

Thus, with palms joined in reverence, he spoke: *Oṃ klīṃ puruṣottama, you who intoxicate the three worlds, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ—salutation to the Heart.* *Oklīṃ sakalajagatkṣobhaṇa, beloved of Lakṣmī, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ—Svāhā to the Head.* *Oṃ klīṃ manmathottamāṅgaja, illuminator of desire, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ—Vaṣaṭ to the Tuft of Hair.* *Oṃ...*

*klīṃ paramasubhage sarvasaubhāgyakare apratirūpake keśava smara huṃ phaṭ namaḥ kavacāya huṃ*. *oṃ klīṃ surāsura-manuja-sundari hṛdaya-vidāraṇe sarva-praharaṇa-dhare sarva-kāmika-hana-hana sarva-hṛdaya-bandhanāni ākarṣaya ākarṣaya mahā-bala-astrāya phaṭ*.

*oṃ klīṃ vibhu-vaneśvara sarva-jana-manāṃsi hana (2) dāraya (2) me vaśam ānaya netratrāya vauṣaṭ*. Thus, one should apply the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*) ending with the eyes, beginning from the thumb and so forth.

Having placed the Netra-mantra on the two little fingers (talāntakarayoḥ), having placed [the mantras] from Hṛdaya to Astra on the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhayoḥ), and having subsequently placed the Netra-mantra, one should perform meditation after having thus placed the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) mantras ending with the Netra. As follows: "First, O Dear One, one should contemplate a garden adorned with all kinds of flowers, resplendent with rows of clusters on numerous small branches, filling the faces of the quarters with the abundance of pollen from its blossoms, containing swarms of bees wandering incessantly, appearing like a marketplace for the sale of fragrance, and [attracting] the senses."

O beloved Goddess, in this [place] which bestows the happiness of liberation, which is almost as delightful as the source of the Self (Brahman), which is like a charming pleasure-palace for the Fortune of Love, which is like the birthplace of the seasons where Rati finds supreme bliss, which is the very model of all beautiful things, the cause of the eyes' fulfillment, and the sole illustration of wondrous phenomena— the practitioner, composed in mind, should remember the Kalpa-tree: its base made of shining sapphire, its trunk formed of fresh diamonds, and...

Having sprinkled the trunk, he beheld the tree whose long branches were like swords and gold, whose mature leaves were emeralds, and whose glistening shoots were bright gems; it bore flowers of priceless jewels with filaments radiant as pearls, from the heart of which issued nectar-like honey. This tree was being praised by swarms of playful bees—bees who, out of passion, had transcended old age—and by throngs of its own nourishers; and it was bestowing upon the multitude of supplicants a flood of wealth in the form of flowing streams of floral nectar.

At the base of that tree, which bore the beauty of streams of flowing nectar and possessed a circle of beautiful, revolving bees for its foliage, there stood the glorious, lotus-eyed Lord, appearing as if he were about to manifest before one's very eyes. He was performing penance, bathed with the waters of celestial flowers, and seated upon the back of Garuḍa, the king of birds, who shone with the brilliance of the sun and rested upon a supreme, reddish-pink lotus situated on a ground of refined ruby dust. Please describe him.

O Maheśvarī, one should remember Him who holds the discus in His hand, whose splendor is equal to ten million suns, who is full of loveliness and radiant with the tenderness of youth; who, by the beauty and majesty of His limbs, puts to shame the pride of Kāmadeva; whose reddish eyes move gently, and who is overwhelmed by the rising arrows of Love; whose body shines with jewel ornaments and is enveloped in divine fragrances; who, with His ruddy luster, colors the entire universe; who is served by hundreds of celestial nymphs, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and gods; and whose beautiful hair is dark and curly.

He was enchanting the assembly of amorous women with his large lotus-petal eyes, his heart-stealing and melodious humming from his longing for the honey-bees, and his form resembling a swarm of bees fluttering about the bow of Kandarpa. He shone with the luster of a great jewel upon his crown; his lips were reddened by a mass of coral-stones and resembled ripe bimba fruits; his nose was as beautiful as a bamboo stalk; his cheeks were illuminated by the brilliance of his swaying earrings; and he was adorned with a garland of shining celestial flowers.

One should meditate on him as having a white neck and arms adorned with jingling bracelets. His fingers, which resemble shining coral and are set with various jewel-studded rings, should be visualized. One should contemplate a discus, radiant as the sun, in the lower right hand; likewise, a sword in the upper [right], and a mace in the one to its left. Similarly, in the upper right hand, one should contemplate a goad; in the upper left, a noose; and below that, a conch. Furthermore, one should meditate on a bow with an arrow in the left [upper] hand, and a mace in the lower left hand.

One should meditate upon the chest of Hari, which is pressed by the breasts of Lakṣmī, vast and beautiful, shining with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; adorned with a charmingly radiant forest garland (vanamālā), it possesses a deep navel-region with a clockwise whorl. One should remember His thick body resplendent with a golden-yellow garment, and His two feet—which resemble red lotuses, are adorned with ruby-like reddish toenails and finger-rings, and possess the signs of the fire, the thunderbolt, and the lotus—shining with anklets, bestowing both knowledge and sovereignty. Or [one may meditate thus].

One should meditate upon the Goddess Brahmī, seated upon a lotus, possessing a radiance like gold; her lotus-feet resound with tinkling anklets, and she is endowed with broad hips and a slender waist. She has beautiful, full, and elevated breasts, and the tips of her arms are adorned with jingling bracelets. She wears various jeweled rings, and her coral-red lips are like the bimba fruit. Her eyes are like blue lotuses, and her long, glossy, dark, curly hair is most radiant.

From the region of her head, she bears a garland of pearls, and she wears swinging earrings and a pair of necklaces reaching down from her throat, shining with strings of pearls. [She dwells in] the Ocean of Milk.

I meditate upon Sarasvatī, who stands embracing the Lord with her right arm, clad in white garments as beautiful as foam; whose bodice of horripilation has quickly arisen from the touch of her beloved’s body;
who, deluded by the arrows of Love, gazes intently at the face of this God; who, on the right side of the God of gods, speaks words consisting of prose and verse;

who holds a lute and a book; whose limbs are smeared with white sandalwood paste; who possesses full and elevated breasts; who is the goddess with wide eyes, adorned with pearl necklaces, and who is creating [the world].

O Goddess of pure smiles, one should meditate with the eyes upon the supreme goddess of the gods, Viṣṇu, for the attainment of knowledge and good fortune; she is the speech of the Lord (Girā). Or, one should meditate on the forms of Hari beginning with Vāsudeva, which are respectively dark, white, reddish, and yellow, adorned with all ornaments. Likewise, one should meditate on the eight Śaktis of the God of gods surrounding him—Lakṣmī and the others—all adorned with every ornament, holding chowries and bracelets, wearing pearl necklaces, possessing slender waists, their lotus-feet adorned with tinkling anklets, and their breasts full and swelling.

Beholding the God who deludes the three worlds, they were afflicted by love: Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, and likewise Aruṇā; Śaśāṅkadhavalā, Jñeyā, Kāntimatī, Tīrthapriyā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Śyāmā, as well as Dhyātavī, who dwells upon the chest of Hari. These women of the lords of clouds, gods, and Daityas, overwhelmed by passion, O Śiva, taking sandalwood and other perfumes, as well as garlands of gold and jewels, came from all sides, longing for the sight of the God. With garlands of golden flowers and various auspicious sandal-pastes, [they worshipped] the Lord of the Three Worlds.

O Beloved, the sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, humans, and lords of men constantly worship Lord Kāma-mohana; O Dear One, they should meditate upon Hari, who is dear to all, as he flows forth from every side, surrounded on all sides by Indra and the other world-protectors, and worshipped by all the worlds from the realm of Brahmā downwards. He resides in a place extending ten million yojanas, fashioned of gold and jewels, which brings delight to the mind, O Goddess, and grants the desires of practitioners. O Goddess, he is established within the three mandalas created by Dharma and the other powers, and abides in the pure and excellent Śaktis beginning with Vimalā.

One should meditate thus upon the Lord seated upon the Gopī-pīṭha of great luster, who deludes all beings, illuminating the worlds with his own radiance; whose multitude of virtues is being drunk in by throngs of Kinnaras, Uragas, Gandharvas, Vāraṇas, and their own followers; and who grants the fulfillment of all desires. Having meditated in this way and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other limbs, offer the recitation to the God, and prostrate before the Guru and the God. This is the Puruṣottama mantra. Now follows the second Puruṣottama mantra.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this thirteen-syllable mantra: *oṃ klīṃ śrīṃ puruṣottamāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī meter (*chandas*) on the mouth; salutation to the deity Puruṣottama on the heart. Having thus assigned [the parts], one says with palms joined in reverence: "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of the desired goal. Then, one performs the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands with these mantras: *oṃ* for the heart, *klīṃ* for the head, *śrīṃ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *puruṣottamāya* for the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ phaṭ* for the eyes, and *svāhā* for the weapon (*astra*).

Having made this arrangement, one should meditate as follows: one should remember Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is red in color, four-armed, and holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. Having meditated—visualizing [the mantras] on the left and right upper arms, and on the first and second lower arms respectively—one should perform the *nyāsa* of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other components at the end of the recitation, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the second Puruṣottama mantra.
Thus ends the sixth section in the *Mantracandrikā*, composed by Gosvāmin Janārdana Bhaṭṭa, son of Gosvāmin Jagannivāsa.

Chapter 6: Now, the mantra of Hṛṣīkeśa: *klīṃ hṛṣīkeśāya namaḥ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this eight-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), upon the head;

salutation to the Anuṣṭubh meter (*chandas*), upon the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Hṛṣīkeśa, upon the heart. Then, saying "for the attainment of desired success, this is the application," and having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) starting with *klīṃ klīm* while joining the palms in reverence, one should meditate as follows: [upon Him] holding the conch, mace, and lotus...

One should meditate on the All-pervading Lord seated upon Garuḍa, white in color and adorned with beautiful ornaments. Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other factors, offer the merit of the recitation, and prostrate. This is the mantra of Hṛṣīkeśa. Now, the mantra of Śrīdhara: *Śrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ śrīdharāya trailokyamohanāya namaḥ*.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this sixteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the assignment (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to Brahmā, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; [salutation to] Śrīdhara on the heart."

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Obeisance to the Deity" (*yad-devatāyai namaḥ*) and having uttered the *mudrā* for the attainment of desired success with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands using the mantras: *Śrāṃ* for the heart, *Śrīṃ* for the head, *Śrūṃ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *Śraiṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *Śrauṃ* for the eyes (*netra*), and *Śraḥ* for the weapon (*astra*). Then, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: In the Ocean of Milk, within a forest frequented by all seasons on a continent, beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpa-druma*), upon a beautiful throne of a lordly bird (*pakṣīndra*) shining with a vast lotus pedestal—[therein is He] holding, with His lotus-like hands, a sword, a mace, and a lotus, [and] properly [bearing] His own... [shield].

"I worship Śrīdhara, who is radiant with the luster of the jewels shining upon his crown. Having meditated thus, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), having performed the placement of the syllables (*nyāsa*) on the eyes and other parts, and having offered the recitation to the Deity, one should prostrate.

This is the Śrīdhara mantra. Now, the Paramātman mantra: "Obeisance to Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda" (11 syllables). Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this eleven-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows:

"Obeisance to the sage Śaunaka on the head; obeisance to the Virāṭ meter on the mouth; obeisance to the deity Paramātman on the heart. Having thus performed the placement, [one should proceed with] the desired...

Having performed the ritual application (*viniyoga*) for the sake of the sixfold perfections (*ṣaṭ-siddhi*), one should, with palms joined in reverence, recite the mantras: "Obeisance to Acyuta, the heart; *svāhā* to Ananta, the head; *vaṣaṭ* to Govinda, the tuft of hair (*śikhā*); *huṃ* to Acyuta, the armor (*kavaca*); *vauṣaṭ* to Ananta, the eyes; *phaṭ* to Govinda, the weapon (*astra*). Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the hands, one should perform meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows:
"The Lord who holds the conch and the discus, four-armed, wearing a crown, endowed with all weapons, seated upon Garuḍa, together with Sanaka and the other lords of sages..."

One should meditate upon the God who is worshipped by all the deities, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, resembling the rising sun; whose earrings are like the orb of the thousand-rayed sun rising at dawn; who is infinite, eternal, the protector of all the worlds, the bestower of fearlessness and boons, and who holds [the conch and discus] while filled with joy. Having thus meditated, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the placement of the Ṛṣi and other limbs, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the procedure for the mantra of the Supreme Self. Now, the Narasiṃha mantra: "The fierce and heroic Great Viṣṇu, blazing, with faces on all sides..."

"I bow to the auspicious Nṛsiṃha, the terrifying one, the death of Death. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra consisting of thirty syllables, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Anuṣṭubh, the Metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the Deity (*devatā*), on the heart. Then, stating "For the attainment of all desired goals, this is the application (*viniyoga*)," one recites: "To the fierce and heroic [one], salutation to the heart; to Mahāviṣṇu, svāhā to the head; to the blazing one facing in all directions, [salutation] to the crest-lock (*śikhā*)."

Having performed the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* on the hands with the mantras: "Vaṣaṭ to the terrifying Nṛsiṃha for the armor, Huṃ; Bhadraṃ Mṛtyumṛtyu for the eyes, Vaiṣaṭ; I bow to the weapon, Phaṭ," one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: "I worship Nṛsiṃha, whose arms reach down to his knees, who has three eyes, and who holds a discus and a conch in his hands. He has the form of a boar, with a head that has swallowed the demons by means of his fierce luster; he is radiant with fangs that beautify [his face], and he has two tongues. In his right and left hands are the discus and the conch. Having meditated thus and performed the recitation (*japa*), at the conclusion of the recitation, one should [assign] the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [limbs].

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*), recited the mantra, and offered the dedication, one should perform prostration. Thus concludes the *Nṛsiṃha-mantra*. Now, the second *Nṛsiṃha-mantra*: having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the single-syllable mantra *KṢAUṂ*, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Atri, the Seer (*ṛṣi*)," on the head; "Salutation to Gāyatrī, the Metre (*chandas*)," on the mouth; "Salutation to Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the Deity (*devatā*)," on the heart. Having thus performed the placement, one should state with palms joined in reverence, "For the attainment of desired success, this is the application (*viniyoga*). Then, the mantra for the six limbs is: *KṢĀṂ* for the heart, *KṢIṂ* for the head, *KṢŪṂ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *KṢAIṂ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *KṢAUṂ* for the eyes (*netra*), and *KṢAḤ* for the weapon (*astra*).

Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and meditated as before on Nṛsiṃha with the mantra beginning "I worship Nṛsiṃha," one should perform the recitation (*japa*). At the conclusion of the recitation, having assigned the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other factors, one should offer the recitation. This is the second Nṛsiṃha mantra. Now, for the third Nṛsiṃha mantra: *Āṃ hrīṃ kṣrauṃ kroṃ huṃ phaṭ*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this six-syllable mantra, one should assign [the limbs] thus:

"Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Paṅkti meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Nṛsiṃha, on the heart. Then, having accomplished one's desired goal...

Having performed the assignment (*viniyoga*) with the heart-mantra, one should recite with palms joined: *Āṃ* for the heart, *Hrūṃ* for the head, *Kṣrauṃ* for the crest (*śikhā*), *Krauṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *Huṃ* for the eyes (*netra*), and *Phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*). Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the hands and body with these six-limbed mantras, one should meditate as follows: May he protect [us]—he whose face is distorted and blazing with wrath, who is red in color, and above the navel bears the moon;

whose three eyes are the moon, the fire, and the sun; who has fierce fangs; and who, with his lotus-like hands, wields the discus, the conch, the noose, the goad, the thunderbolt, the mace, and the weapon known as the *Dāraṇa*.

The Man-Lion (Vānṛsiṃha), possessing a terrifying body and adorned with various clusters of jewels, has [the first] two hands on the right side raised upward, the next two placed below them, and the others placed below those;

from the two lowest hands, there is the *Dāraṇa-mudrā*. As for the characteristic of the *Dāraṇa-mudrā*: "The fingers, joined together and facing each other, are straight and downward-pointing; the thumbs remain in their own positions, straightened—this mudrā is known as *Dāraṇa*. Thus is the meditation on the weapons (*āyudha-dhyāna*). Having meditated thus and performed recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Ṛṣis and so forth.

Having offered the recitation (*japa*) and prostrated, this concludes the third *Nṛsiṃha-mantra*. Now follows the fourth *Nṛsiṃha-mantra*: *Oṃ kṣrauṃ namo bhagavate nārasiṃhāya jvālāmāline dīptadaṃṣṭrāyāgninetrāya sarvarakṣoghnāya sarvabhūtavināśāya sarvajvaravināśaya daha daha paca paca rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā.* Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra of sixty-seven syllables, one should offer salutations: "Salutation to Prajāpati, the Ṛṣi, upon the head; [to Gāyatrī, the metre,] upon the mouth... [and so forth].

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the one who has come; obeisance to the Lord Śrī Nṛsiṃha," and having said with palms joined, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of desired goals," [one recites]:

"Oṃ Kṣrauṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Heart of Narasiṃha, obeisance! Svāhā to the flaming garlanded one with blazing fangs, the Head! Vaṣaṭ to the fire-eyed one, the destroyer of all Rākṣasas, the Tuft (Śikhā)! Huṃ to the armor (*kavaca*) which destroys all beings and destroys all fevers! Dahadaha! Pacapaca! Rakṣarakṣa me!"

Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantra *trāyavauṣaṭ huṃ phaṭ svāhā astrāya phaṭ*, one should meditate as follows: "I bow to the glorious Nṛsiṃha, the destroyer of the Daityas, who is always being praised by hosts of sages and gods; who possesses the luster of the rising fire of cosmic destruction (*kālānala*); whose mouth is fierce with fangs blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon; who is terrifying with the mass of his thick, dark manes beautiful as streaks of lightning; who has three eyes; and who holds in his lotus-like hands a sword, a discus, a shield, and a mace. The visualization of the weapons begins from the upper left and proceeds downwards: [sword], [shield], [mace], and [discus].

Having meditated with the meaning "the excellent sword of the poor," having performed the recitation (*japa*), and having performed the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other factors, one should offer the recitation. This is the fourth *Nṛsiṃha* mantra. Now, the *Śrī-Nṛsiṃha* mantra: *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ japalakṣmīpriyāya nityapramuditacetase lakṣmīśrītārddhadehāya śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ*.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this thirty-three-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: *Namaḥ to Prajāpati, the Ṛṣi, on the head*; *Namaḥ to Anuṣṭubh, the metre, on the mouth*; *Hṛdayāya...* [on the heart]. *Śrī...* [on the heart].

"Obeisance to the deity Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha"—having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of one's desired goal. Having formed the hollowed palms of the hands and performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands with the aforementioned mantras beginning with *kṣrīṃ kṣrīṃ m* and so forth, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: "The supreme Nṛsiṃha, whose abode is the coils of the lord of serpents, who has a beautiful canopy of excellent hoods, who is radiant like lightning and the moon, who is embraced by the Supreme Goddess (Caramā), who possesses divine ornaments on all four sides, and who holds in his hands the gestures of granting boons (*vara*), discus (*ari*), lotus (*kamala*), and fearlessness (*abhaya*)—beginning from the lower right hand... [and so on].

The meditation on the weapons extends down to the lower hands. Thus, at the conclusion of the meditation and recitation, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣi* and other elements, one should offer the recitation to the Deity and perform prostration. This concludes the Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha mantra. Now follows the second Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha mantra: *Oṃ Śrī Lakṣmīnṛsiṃhāya*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this eight-syllable mantra, one should place the mantras as follows:
"Salutation to Prajāpati, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to the *anuṣṭubh* meter on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha on the heart."

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with *kṣrāṃ kṣrīṃ* and so forth, and having meditated as before on [the Lord] "whose abode is the coils of the lord of serpents" (*sarpendrabhog-nilaya*), at the end of the recitation, one should perform the placement of the Seer (*ṛṣi*) and others and offer the recitation. This is the second *Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha* mantra. Now, the third *Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha* mantra: having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the eight-syllable mantra "Japa japa śrī nṛsiṃha," the Seer, the six limbs, and so forth are to be performed as in the previously mentioned eight-syllable mantra. This is the third [mantra], Nṛsiṃha.

Now, another *Nṛsiṃha* mantra: *Kṣrauṃ matsyāya kṣrauṃ, kūrmāya kṣrauṃ, varāhāya kṣrauṃ, nṛsiṃhāya kṣrauṃ, vāmanāya kṣrauṃ, rāmāya kṣrauṃ, rāmāya kṣrauṃ, rāmāya kṣrauṃ, kṛṣṇāya kṣrauṃ, kalkine japa japa śālagrāmanivāsine divyasiṃha svayaṃbhu-puruṣāya namaḥ kṣrauṃ*.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this sixty-nine-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to Atri, the seer (*ṛṣi*)" on the head; "Salutation to Atichandas" on the mouth; "Salutation to Śrī Nṛsiṃha" on the heart.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Hāyadevatāyai namaḥ," and having executed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with "Kṣrāṃ Kṣrīṃ" and so forth, one should meditate upon Nṛsiṃha according to the previously mentioned Nṛsiṃha mantra beginning with "I worship Nṛsiṃha, whose knees are placed... and perform the recitation (*japa*). Having performed the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and others in a low voice, one should offer the recitation to the deity. This is the Nṛsiṃha mantra.
Now, three other mantras are written here: Oṃ namo bhagavate vīranṛsiṃhāya jvālāmālāpinaddhāṅgāya agnine-trāya sarvabhūtavināśanāya daha daha.

*Paca paca rakṣa rakṣa rakṣa hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra consisting of fifty-two syllables. *Oṃ namo bhagavate vīranṛsiṃhāya jvālāmāline dīptadaṃṣṭrāya agninetrāya sarvarakṣoghnāya sarvabhūtavināśanāya sarvajvaraṃ vināśaya hana hana daha daha paca paca bandha bandha rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra consisting of seventy-four syllables. *Oṃ namo bhagavate vīranṛsiṃhāya jvālāmāline dīptadaṃṣṭrāya agni...* [The text continues with the same invocation].

*Netrāya sarvabhūtavināśanāya sarvajvaravināśanāya sarvadoṣavināśanāya hana hana daha daha paca paca bandha bandha rakṣa māṅgāṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā.* This is the mantra of eighty syllables. For these three mantras as well, the seer (*ṛṣi*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and other details should be understood to be the same as those previously stated for the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*). Thus end the three mantras of Vīranṛsiṃha. Now, another Nṛsiṃha mantra: *Oṃ kṣrauṃ mahānṛsiṃhāya namaḥ*. With this ten-syllable mantra, one should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Vāmadeva on the head; salutation to the Virāṭ metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Nṛsiṃha in the heart. Having said, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of my desired goal," while joining the palms in reverence, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with *kṣrāṃ*, *kṣrīm*, and so forth. Then, having meditated upon the previously mentioned eight-syllabled Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha mantra beginning with "The abode of the coils of the lord of serpents, possessing beautiful hoods... and so on, and having performed the placement of the ṛṣis and others at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should conclude the rite.

Now follows another *Nṛsiṃha* mantra: *Oṃ kṣrauṃ namo bhagavate nṛsiṃhāya*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this thirteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Vāmadeva on the head; salutation to the *Jagatī* meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Nṛsiṃha in the heart. Then, one performs the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with *kṣrīṃ kṣrīṃ mi*, and so forth. As for the meditation (*dhyāna*), one should meditate according to the previously mentioned six-syllable mantra, beginning with "He whose face is expanded and blazing with wrath," and then perform the recitation (*japa*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣi* and other components, one should carry out the recitation (*japa*). This is another *Nṛsiṃha* mantra. Now follows the *Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha* mantra: *oṃ sahasrāra-jvālāvartine kṣauṃ hana-hana huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this nineteen-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement as follows: "Salutation to the *ṛṣi* [Jaimini] on the head; salutation to the *gāyatrī* meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī-Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha in the heart. Having stated the application (*viniyoga*), [one should meditate upon] the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*).
"Oṃ *jāyahṛdayāya* namaḥ; *jvālācakrāya śirase* svāhā; *jagaccakrāya śikhāyai* vaṣaṭ; *asurāntakacakrāya kavacāya* huṃ;

*mahāsudarśanāya astrāya* phaṭ. Having thus assigned these five-limbed mantras (*pañcāṅga-mantra*) to the fingers of his hands consecrated by the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), and having also assigned them to the five limbs beginning with the heart—excluding the eyes—he should perform meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: "In the center of the seat of the discus (*cakrāsana*), [he sees the Lord] whose splendor is like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālāgni*), four-armed, with an open mouth, and four..."

One should meditate upon Hari, the wielder of the discus, whose complexion shines like the moon and lightning, who has three eyes and a formidable form, and who destroys the flood of all miseries, diseases, and poverty. Having thus meditated, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other factors, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the *Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha* mantra. Now, the mantras of Rāma are being described.

First, the single-syllable mantra of Rāma: *Rāṃ*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this single-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth."

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Obeisance to Śrī Rāma, the Lord of the Heart; obeisance to the Deity," and having declared the application (*viniyoga*), one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) as follows: *Aiṃ* for the heart, *Aiṃ* for the head, *Rūṃ* for the tuft of hair, *Raik* for the armor, *Raun* for the eyes, and *Raḥ* for the weapon. Then one should meditate as follows: On a lotus seat upon a mandāra altar by the banks of the Sarayū, seated in the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), dark-complexioned, adorned with the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa joined to him—Sītā resting on his left thigh—he gazes at himself within his own self, he of immeasurable splendor.

Having meditated thus: "Resembling pure crystal, [I am] absolute," and having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs], offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the single-syllable *Namaḥ* mantra. Now, the two-syllable *Rāma* mantra: Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the mantra "Rām," and having assigned the sage (*muni*) and others as prescribed for the single-syllable [mantra], one should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with "Rāṃ, Rīṃ," and so forth. Then, having meditated upon [the deity] as previously described for the single-syllable [mantra], starting with "Sarayūtīramaṃdāra," one should perform the recitation.

Having performed the ritual procedure, one should conclude it; such is the two-syllabled Rāma-mantra. Now, the three-syllabled Rāma-mantra: that [mantra] is sixfold, consisting of the seed-syllables of Tāra (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Ramā (Śrīṃ), Anaṅga (Klīṃ), Vāk (Aiṃ), and Svā (Svā).

Thus: Oṃ Rāmaḥ, Hrīṃ Rāmaḥ, Śrīṃ Rāmaḥ, Klīṃ Rāmaḥ, Roṃ Rāmaḥ, Roṃ Rāmaḥ. Now, the four-syllabled Rāma-mantras: "Rāmabhadra" is one four-syllabled mantra, and "Rāmacandra" is another four-syllabled mantra. For the three- and four-syllabled mantras, having performed everything else—the seer, meditation, the six limbs, and so forth—just as in the case of the single-syllabled Rāma-mantra, one should conclude.

Now, there are mantras of three and four syllables. Next is the five-syllable mantra of Rāma: *Rāmāya namaḥ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to Viśvāmitra, the Ṛṣi," on the head; "Salutation to Paṅkti, the metre (*chandas*)," on the mouth; "Salutation to Rāmabhadra, the deity (*devatā*)," on the heart; "Salutation to *rāṃ*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*)," on the private parts; and "Salutation to *namaḥ*, the power (*śakti*)," on the feet. Then, with *rāṃ rīṃ* and so forth, one should assign: *rāṃ* to the head, *rīṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *ūṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *aiṃ* to the eyes, and "Salutation to Rāma" (*rāmāya namaḥ*). To the weapon (*astra*).

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the *stramiti* mantras, one should perform meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows: "In the middle of a forest, at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), upon a seat of flowers and creepers, one should meditate on the Lord who is being fanned by Jānakī while Lakṣmaṇa holds an arrow against the corner of his eye; whose head is radiant with a mass of matted locks (*jaṭā*); who is dark-complexioned and surrounded by hosts of sages; or else, seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot, holding an umbrella over him, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, and Vibhīṣaṇa—the destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, appearing peaceful. Having meditated thus according to the [tradition]...

Having performed the *kṛtijapa* (the recitation with the ritual procedure), at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā*, offer the merit of the recitation (*japasamarpaṇa*), and prostrate. This is the five-syllabled mantra of Rāma. Now follows the six-syllabled mantra of Rāma. It consists of five syllables preceded by the seed-syllable of one’s own desire (*svakāma*), the *śakti*, *vā*, *lakṣmī*, or *tāra*; thus, the six-syllabled mantra is of six types. They are as follows: (1) *Rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ* (2) *Klīṃ rāmāya namaḥ* (3) *Hrīṃ rāmāya namaḥ* (4) *Roṃ rāmāya namaḥ* (5) *Śrīṃ rāmāya namaḥ* (6) *Oṃ rāmāya namaḥ* In this way, the six-syllabled mantra is of six kinds.

Or else, preceded by each of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā-mantra, it may be preceded by Lakṣmī (Śrī), Vāyu (Vā), Manmatha (Kāma), and so forth; thus it becomes manifold. As follows: "With two lotus-hands granting boons and fearlessness..."

Meditate thus: [He] whose limbs are dear to His consort, who joyfully embraces her with hands adorned with lotuses and water-lilies, who holds the discus (rathāṅga) and possesses a beautiful body like a conch shell.

In this mantra, the placement (*nyāsa*) is said to consist of twenty syllables, while that described for the ten-syllable mantra is as follows. Having meditated thus upon the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other components, one should recite the mantra ten hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind. One should offer the finest clarified butter (*ājya*) in that same number of thousands. Through libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites, the mantra becomes perfected and bestows one's desired fruits—thus it is stated in the *Vidyārṇava*. Having performed the recitation according to the prescribed rule, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the seer and other components, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the sixteen-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa. Now [follows]...

The twelve-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa is: *hrīṃ śrīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the other rites, such as the satisfaction of the elements (*tṛpyādi*), as in the case of the sixteen-syllable mantra. Thus ends the twelve-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa. Now, the thirteen-syllable mantras of Kṛṣṇa: First: *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. Second:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. Third: *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*.

Having performed the *ṛṣi*-assignment and other preliminary rites for these mantras as was done for the previously mentioned ten-syllable Gopāla mantra, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) for the third mantra as was done for the ten-syllable mantra, the meditation for the second mantra as was done for the previously mentioned twenty-syllable mantra, and then perform the meditation for the first mantra as follows: For the attainment of desired fruits, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa situated within the solar disc, filled with joy, holding a flute in his two hands and playing it, while his lotus-like hands hold a bow, arrows, a bowstring, and a goad. Thus [is the meditation] for the first mantra.

Having performed meditation (*dhyāna*) and recitation (*japa*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣi* and other components, one should offer salutations to the serpent-like [deity] after the recitation. Thus, there are three eleven-syllable Kṛṣṇa-mantras. Now, the eleven-syllable Kṛṣṇa-mantra: *gopījanavallabhāya svāhā klīṃ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement as follows: "Salutation to Nārada, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart. Then, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with *klāṃ klīṃ* and so forth, one should meditate.

Furthermore, one should meditate upon the beautiful son of Nanda, who possesses the splendor of a magnificent blue luster, holding in his right lotus-hand a ripe *dogdhaka* fruit; and in his left hand, a beautiful, auspicious curd-bowl produced on that very day, its neck adorned with a tiger’s claw-mark and his garment cast aside. Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the seers (*ṛṣis*) and other limbs, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the eleven-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa. Now, the twenty-two-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa...

The mantra (for its worship, twenty syllables are prescribed): *aiṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya hrīṃ goviṃdāya śrīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā sauḥ*. Having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to Brahmā, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the Meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Deity (*devatā*), on the heart. Then, one should assign the five-limbed mantras: *aiṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* for the heart; *hrīṃ goviṃdāya* for the head; *śrīṃ gopījana* for the tuft (*śikhā*); *vallabhāya* for the armor (*kavaca*); and *svāhā sauḥ* for the weapon (*astra*). [These are assigned] from the thumb to the little finger.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the fingers and likewise on the five limbs beginning with the heart—excluding the eyes—one should meditate as follows: May that enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) be for my prosperity—he who is dark-complexioned with tender limbs, clad in yellow garments, and possessing the beauty of a mass of hair bound with peacock feathers; who holds in his upper right lotus-hand a crystal rosary in the form of the letters of the *Mātṛkā*, and in his upper left hand a fresh book containing all branches of knowledge; and who, sounding the single flute of the *Śabdabrahman* held by his pair of hands, sings of Yoga like Śrī herself. May he be endowed with the splendor of a mass of hair bound with peacock feathers.

Then, having meditated upon the Lord of Devas—who is served by the entire multitude of sages from all sides, who is omniscient, and who is to be visualized wearing female attire (*nepathya*)—that is, wearing the ornaments of a woman; having thus meditated, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other components, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the twenty-two-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa.
Now follows the twenty-eight-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa: *oṃ namo bhagavate nandaputrāya nandavapuṣe śrīgopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. Thus is the mantra.

Having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to the *uṣṇih* meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity, the son of Śrī Nanda, in the heart. Having thus performed the placement, one should assign the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) using the previously mentioned ten-syllable Gopāla mantra beginning with *ā-cakra*. Then, having meditated—visualizing Kṛṣṇa joyfully embraced by two women, holding a jewel-vessel in his right hand and a flute in his left—one should, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), perform the placement of the sage and other elements and offer the recitation.

Thus ends the mantra of twenty-eight syllables. Now follows the Kṛṣṇa-mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables: *naṃdaputrāyāśyāmalāṅgāyavālavapuṣekṛṣṇāyagoviṃdāyagopījanavallabhāyasvāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh meter in the mouth;

salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the heart. Then, having performed the five-limbed placement (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*) as before with the discus and other symbols, one should fill the jewel-vessel with water.

Having meditated as prescribed, at the end of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other components and offer the recitation. Thus ends the thirty-two-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa. Now follows the forty-two-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa:

*oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ namo bhagavate nandaputrāya bālavapuṣe śyāmalāṅgāya klīṃ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should place the salutations: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*)" on the head; "Salutation to the Anuṣṭubh meter" on the mouth; and "Salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa" on the heart.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Oṃ namaḥ to the deity of the bath," and having made the *viniyoga* (application) for the attainment of desired success while joining the palms in reverence, one should recite: "Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the son of Nanda—[this is] the heart;
to the one with a youthful body—[this is] the head; to the dark-limbed one—[this is] the crest-lock; to Kṛṣṇa Govinda, the beloved of the cowherd women, Svāhā—[this is] the armor.

Having thus consecrated the two hands with the root mantra, one should perform the placement on the fingers from the thumb to the little finger, and on the heart and other limbs (excluding the eyes), using the same sequence.

Having visualized the jewel-bowl [as described] as being like the previously mentioned eighteen-syllable Kṛṣṇa mantra beginning with *dakṣiṇa*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*), at its conclusion one should assign the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other components, offer the recitation, and prostrate.

This is the forty-two-syllable Kṛṣṇa mantra. Now, the sixteen-syllable Kṛṣṇa mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate rukmiṇīvallabhāya svāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should assign: "Salutation to Nārada, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; [salutation] to Śrī Rukmiṇīvallabha on the heart."

Having performed the five-limbed ritual placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) as follows: "Obeisance to the deity Kṛṣṇa" for the heart; "Oṃ, obeisance to the Heart" for the head; "To the Blessed One" for the tuft (*śikhā*); "To the Beloved of Rukmiṇī" for the armor (*kavaca*); and "Svāhā" for the weapon (*astra*). Then one should meditate as follows: One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, adorned with a peacock-feather crown and various ornaments, wearing a fine yellow silken garment, and decorated with a golden staff.

With His right lotus-hand He embraces the Goddess, who sits upon His lap, possesses a golden luster, holds a lotus in Her left hand, and is adorned with a multitude of gems. He is embraced by another [consort] with Her beloved.

Having meditated thus, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other limbs and offer the recitation. This is the sixteen-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa. Now follows the twenty-nine-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa: "Līlā-daṇḍa-gopī-jana-saṃrakṣa-kṣudra-do-daṇḍa-vāla-rūpa-megha-śyāma-bhagavan-Viṣṇo Svāhā. Having performed the three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows:
"Salutation to Nārada, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Līlā-daṇḍa Mahāviṣṇu, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the five limbs with the mantra: "O Lord, whose staff for play (*līlā-daṇḍa*) is held by the Gopīs, whose head is that of a child, who is dark as a rain cloud, O Viṣṇu, [grant] armor, svāhā," one should meditate as follows: One should remember Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable prowess, the Great Lord, who is enchanting the cowherd girls and the cities with the playful staff held in his lotus-like left hand, and who has placed his other hand upon the shoulder of his dear friend Balarāma, holding a plow. Having meditated thus...

Having performed the recitation of the *śakti* mantra and, at the conclusion of the recitation, having assigned the *ṛṣi* and other elements, one should offer the recitation. This is the twenty-nine-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa. Now follows the seven-syllable "Beloved" (*govallabha*) mantra of Kṛṣṇa: *Govallabhāya svāhā*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the assignment of the limbs (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Nārada, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to *uṣṇih* meter on the mouth; salutation to Govallabha Hari, the deity, on the heart. The five limbs [are assigned] with the mantras beginning with the *ā-cakra*, as previously described for the ten-syllable Gopāla mantra.
One should meditate upon Acyuta, who possesses the radiant luster of a sapphire, is clad in yellow garments, and has his head beautifully adorned with a crest of peacock feathers;

who holds a flute in his left hand and a staff and a noose in his right; who stands amidst a flock of tawny cows and joyfully beckons them. Having thus meditated and performed the placement of the *ṛṣi* and other elements at the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer the prayer. This is the seven-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved of the Cow. Now follows the twelve-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa: *Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīgovindāya*.

Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas* with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to the *gāyatrī* metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the heart. Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should state: "This is the application for the attainment of desired success. Next, having performed the five-limbed mantra placement—*oṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ* to the head, *bhagavate* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *śrīgoviṃdāya* to the armor (*kavaca*), and *huṃ oṃ namo bhagavate śrīgoviṃdāya* as the weapon (*astra*)—one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) as follows:

I worship Hari, who has a body dark as a young ram, who wears very thick garments, and who holds a staff and a water-pot in His two hands; whose eyes are as broad as lotuses, and who is the ultimate abode of beauty; and who is being sprinkled by a stream of nectar flowing from the excellent golden pitcher held in the pair of hands of the Lord of the Gods (Indra). Having meditated thus—[the staff in the right hand and the conch in the left]—and having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other limbs at the conclusion of the recitation, offer the recitation, and prostrate. This is the twelve-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇa.

[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Mantracandrikā* composed by Gosvāmī Janārdana, son of Gosvāmī Jagannivāsa. (8) Now follows the eight-syllabled mantra of Gokulanātha: "Oṃ *gokulanāthāya namaḥ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī meter (*chandas*), on the face; salutation to the deity Śrī Gokulanātha, on the heart. Having thus declared the application (*viniyoga*), [one should meditate upon] Gokula-hṛt-lanāśi...

Having performed the assignment of the five limbs (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*) as follows: *raḥ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *namaḥ* to the armor (*kavacaṃ*), *namaḥ gokulanāthāya* to the weapon (*astraṃ*), one should meditate as follows: "I salute the son of Yaśodā, the delight of the assembly of sages, who possesses a beautiful dark-blue complexion endowed with great luster; who has hair like a mass of curls, eyes reddened by crying, and five limbs; who runs about in the courtyard with a girdle, anklets, jeweled necklaces, and armlets, shining brilliantly and moving restlessly. Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, at the conclusion of the recitation, [one should perform] the *ṛṣyā-*... [etc.]

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs and offered the recitation (*japa*) to the Deity, one should prostrate. Thus ends the eight-syllabled mantra of Gokulanātha. Now follows the Siddhagopāla mantra:

*oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ kṛṣṇāya śrīgovindāya śrīgopījanavallabhāya śrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this twenty-five-syllabled mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Siddhagopāla in the heart. Thus having performed the placement:

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with *klīṃ klīṃ* and so forth, one should meditate as follows: "One should remember the two divine Kṛṣṇas, who are sporting in a state of divine being within the Mādhavī bower, served by the multitude of attendants and Garuḍa. Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, one should assign the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other components at the end of the recitation and offer the recitation. This is the Siddha-Gopāla mantra. Alternatively, there is the Bāla-Gopāla mantra: the single syllable *kṛḥ*; the two syllables *kṛṣṇi*; the three syllables *oṃ kṛṣṇi*; and the four syllables *oṃ kṛṣṇāya*.

*Kṣarakṣaraḥ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ* is the five-syllable mantra. *Gopālāya svāhā* is the six-syllable mantra. *Klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā* is the second six-syllable mantra. *Kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya* is the seven-syllable mantra. *Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ* is the second seven-syllable mantra. *Klīṃ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya* is the eight-syllable mantra. *Dadhibhakṣaṇāya svāhā* is the second eight-syllable mantra. *Suprasannātmane namaḥ* is the third eight-syllable mantra. *Klīṃ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya klīṃ* is the [fourth]... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a longer list of mantras; the final portion is incomplete.)

The nine-syllable mantra is: *vākṣaraḥ kṛṣṇāya govindāya namaḥ*. The second nine-syllable mantra is: *klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ śyāmalāṅgāya namaḥ*. The ten-syllable mantra is: *vālavapuṣe kṛṣṇāya svāhā*. The second ten-syllable mantra is:

*klīṃ kṛṣṇāya vālavapuṣe svāhā*. The eleven-syllable mantra is: *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya vālavapuṣe svāhā*. Among these mantras, having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with whichever mantra has been taught to oneself, one should offer salutations: to the sage Nārada upon the head (*śirasi*), to the Goddess Gāyatrī meter in the mouth (*mukhe*), and to Śrī Gopāla in the heart (*hṛdaye*).

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Obeisance to the Deity," and having stated the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of desired success with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) beginning with *klāṃ klīm* and so forth, and then meditate as follows:

One should meditate upon Lord Mukunda, whose abode is the lotus, whose eyes have the luster of red lotuses, and who possesses the splendor of a blue water-lily; who is bound at his waist by a network of tinkling bells;

who holds in his two hands a fresh lotus and sweet milk-rice (*pāyasa*) sprinkled with sugar-cane juice; and who is white with large toenails, while the region of his throat is surrounded by a multitude of cows, cowherd girls, and cowherds.

Having meditated thus—"In the beautiful [place], [I offer] the butter produced from curd"—and having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should assign the *ṛṣi* and other components, offer the recitation, and prostrate.

This is the *Siddha-Gopāla-mantra*. Alternatively, there is the *Bāla-Gopāla-mantra*: The one-syllabled is *Kṛḥ*. The two-syllabled is *Kṛṣṇa*. The three-syllabled is *Oṃ Kṛṣṇa*. The four-syllabled is *Oṃ Kṛṣṇāya*. The five-syllabled is *Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya Klīṃ*. The six-syllabled is *Gopālāya Svāhā*. The second six-syllabled is *Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya Svāhā*.

"Kṣaraḥ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya"—this is a seven-syllable mantra. "Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ"—this is the second seven-syllable mantra. "Klīṃ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya"—this is an eight-syllable mantra. "Dadhibhakṣaṇāya svāhā"—this is the second eight-syllable mantra. "Suprasannātmane namaḥ"—this is the third eight-syllable mantra. "Klīṃ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya klīṃ"—this is a nine-syllable mantra. "Kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya namaḥ"—this is the second nine-syllable mantra. "Klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ śyāmalāṅgāya namaḥ"—this is [the next].

"Śākṣaraḥ vālavapuṣe kṛṣṇāya svāhā" is the second mantra, consisting of ten syllables; "klīṃ kṛṣṇāya vālavapuṣe svāhā" is the [third] mantra, consisting of eleven syllables. Having performed three rounds of *prāṇāyāma* with one of these mantras—specifically the mantra taught to oneself—one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head (*śiras*); salutation to the goddess Gāyatrī meter in the mouth (*mukha*); salutation to the deity Śrī Gopāla in the heart (*hṛdaya*). Then, with palms joined in reverence, one declares the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of desired success, beginning with "klāṃ klīm," and so forth.

Having performed the Kara-ṣaḍaṅga Nyāsa, one should meditate upon Lord Mukunda as follows: He is seated upon a lotus, his eyes possess the luster of a red lotus, and his complexion is like that of a blue water-lily. His waist is bound with a network of tinkling bells, and with his two hands he holds fresh curd and sweet milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar-cane juice. He is surrounded by a multitude of cows, cowherds, and cowherdesses; and on his beautiful neck, he wears fresh butter (navanīta) from curd, which has been pressed out by his large, long nails. Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (japa) according to one's capacity, and having assigned the Ṛṣi and other limbs at the end of the recitation, one should offer the japa and prostrate.

Now, following the *Itivṛttaka* and *Gopāla-mantras*, here is another *Vālagopāla-mantra*: *klīṃ kṛṣṇa klīṃ*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this four-syllabled mantra and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as previously described, one should meditate as follows: "I bow to Mukunda, who sits upon a blossoming lotus at the foot of the glorious divine tree; from whose branch, which is bent down by joy, fall many jewels from the blooming lotuses; whose golden-colored form is embraced by the world of Vyāsa through the splendor shining from his own body; and who bestows the destruction of sins. I bow to Him who is born from the curd-ocean.

Having meditated thus: "He who eats fresh food and is of excellent character," one should perform the *nyāsa* of the sages (*ṛṣi*) and others at the end of the recitation and offer the recitation (*japa*). This is another mantra of Bālagopāla. Now, for yet another mantra of Bālagopāla:

having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the four-syllabled mantra "klīṃ kṛṣṇa klīṃ" as before, and having performed the *nyāsa* of the sages and others, one should perform the six-limbed *nyāsa* (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) starting with "klāṃ klām" and so forth, and then meditate as follows: "On the peak of the divine tree in the red garden, he has come to the golden swing; he is dark-blue..."

I bow to the son of Yaśodā, the enemy of Mura, who is exceedingly beautiful, whose hair is curled, who is adorned with tinkling bells at his waist, who wears a necklace fashioned from the claws of a red tiger, and who is joyfully swaying between two gopīs. Having thus meditated, performed the recitation (*japa*), and assigned the *ṛṣi* and other components, one should offer the recitation. This is another mantra for Bālagopāla. Now, the mantra of Saṃmohana Gopāla: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ṭrīṃ nrīṃ jrīṃ jhrīṃ jaya jaya kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa nirantarakrīḍāsaktapramuditacetasa...* (O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, you whose mind is perpetually delighted and attached to play...)

Having performed the three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with this fifty-two-syllable mantra: *tasainityapriyāyakṛṣṇāyaklīṃgopījanavallabhāyasvāhā śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows:

"Salutation to the sage Ānandanārada on the head; salutation to the immortal Virāṭ metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrīsaṃmohanakṛṣṇa in the heart. Having said, "This is for the application toward the attainment of all my desired goals," while joining the palms in reverence (*añjali*), [one recites]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ṭrīṃ nrīṃ jrīṃ jhrīṃ jaya jaya śrīṃ*.
