Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the mantra "śvānāva siṃdhuṃ duritāty agniḥ" (which consists of forty-three syllables), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Kaśyapa on the head; salutation to the *triṣṭubh* meter on the mouth; salutation to the deity Agni Jātavedas on the heart. Then, having recited the application (*viniyoga*), one should assign the mantras: "To Jātavedas, we offer [oblations], salutation to the heart; 'Soma from the enemy,' svāhā to the head; 'May he burn away the knower,' vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); 'May he carry us across... [and so forth].

Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantras: "cāyahuṃ durgāṇi viśvā nāveva netrāya vauṣaṭ" and "siṃdhuṃ duritāty agniḥ astrāya phaṭ," one should meditate as follows:

"I meditate upon Durgā, who has three eyes, whose radiance is like a garland of lightning, who stands upon the shoulders of the Lord of Beasts (Śiva), who is awe-inspiring, and who is attended by maidens whose hands gleam with swords and shields;
she holds in her hands a discus, a mace, a sword, a shield, arrows, a bow, a goad, and a threatening gesture, and she bears the wind, fire, and the moon."

One should meditate on the weapons as follows: "The first [weapon] is on the right and left shoulders; the second is on the lower part of those two; the third is on the upper part of those two; the others are on the remaining [limbs].

Having thus meditated and performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other factors and offer the recitation. This is the mantra known as Āgneya.
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the *Mantracandrikā* composed by Śrī Gosvāmī Janārdana Bhaṭṭa, son of Śrī Gosvāmī Jagan-nivāsa. Thus ends the section on Śiva.]

[End. Now, having thus written the mantras, one should examine their states as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, or *ari*. The wheel (*cakra*) is described: in the *Lakṣmīkulārṇava*, one should write the syllables of the Goddess in sequence within the cells—namely one, three, eleven, nine, two, four, twelve, one, six, eight, sixteen, fourteen, five, seven, and fifteen.
One (1), three (3), Rudra (11), nine (9), Netra (2), Yuga (4), Arka (12), Paṅkti (10), Ṣaṭ (6), Nāga (8).

The remaining [letters] are sixteen (16), fourteen (14), five (5), seven (7), fifteen (15), and thirteen (13). From the *mātṛkā*—the alphabet—one should take the letters of the goddess Ambikā numbering three, three, and nine. Now, the method for constructing this wheel (*cakra*): having drawn five lines extending east-west and five lines extending north-south, one forms sixteen squares. These squares are then grouped into four sets of four squares each, forming four clusters of four.

In the four squares of the northeast (Īśāna) quadrant of the eightfold [mandala], starting from the northeast square and moving clockwise: *ka, tha, ha* (0); *u, ḍa, pa, nṛ, jha, ma* (0); *o, ḍa, vā, gne, ya, ca, tu, ṣke*; *ī, śā, nā, di, pra, da, kṣi, ṇye*.

In the southeast (Āgneya) quadrant, starting from the northeast and moving clockwise: *a, kha, da, la*; *ū, ca, pha, ḷ, ja, ṣa*; *au, ṭha, śaḥ*; *ni, ṛ, ti, ca, tu, ṣke*. In the southwest (Nairṛti) quadrant, starting from the northeast and moving clockwise: *i, ga, dha, kṣa*; *ṛ, cha, ba*; *e, ṭa, raḥ*; *aṃ, ṇa, ṣa*. In the fourth (northwest) quadrant, starting from the northeast and moving clockwise: *ṇi, ṣa, nṛ, ja, bha*; *ai, ṭha, la* (0); *aḥ, ta*.

Having written all the letters of the Mātṛkā in order, one should count from the square where the first letter of the disciple’s name resides until the square containing the first letter of the mantra; having thus counted, one should examine whether the mantra is *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, or *ari*. In that regard, if the first letter of the practitioner’s name and the first letter of the mantra reside in the same square, the mantra is known as *siddha*. If the first letter of the mantra is in the second square [relative to the disciple’s name], the mantra is *siddhasādhya*. If it is in the third, it is *siddha*.

If [the mantra] is *susiddha* in the fourth [cell], it is an enemy (*ari*) of the *siddha*. Even in the second group of four, one should assume the first cell to be the same as the [original] first cell and count from there in a clockwise direction.

If the first letter of the mantra stands in the first cell, then that mantra is a *siddha-sādhya*; in the second, it is a *sādhya-sādhya*; in the third, a *sādhya-susiddha*; and in the fourth, a *sādhya-ari*. Likewise, in the third group of four, [if the first letter is in] the first cell, it is *susiddha*; in the second, *susiddha-sādhya*; in the third, *susiddha-su*... [and so on].

In the fourth [square], the enemy is "Siddha" (accomplished). Thus, even in the fourth group of four, if the first letter of the mantra is in the first square, then the enemy is "Siddha"; if in the second, the enemy is "Sādhya" (to be accomplished); if in the third, the enemy is "Susiddha" (well-accomplished); and if in the fourth, the enemy is "Ari" (enemy). Having thus investigated and understood this correctly, one should perform the union of mantras; otherwise, the mantra will become a source of misfortune. For there is a saying in the *Yāmala-valaya*: "There is no friend equal to a mantra, and there is no enemy equal to a mantra. Now, the results of these are described in the *Kulāmūlāvatāra*.

A *siddha-siddha* [mantra] is accomplished through a long period of time; a *sādhya-siddha* is accomplished without delay; and a *susiddha-siddha* accomplishes its purpose at that very moment. An enemy [of the mantra], being a *mūla-siddha*, cuts off one's very root. In the *Tantrarāja*: A *siddha-siddha* is accomplished through recitation (*japa*). A *sādhya-siddha* is accomplished with double the effort. When a *susiddha-siddha* is attained, it grants success. An enemy of the *siddha* (i.e., a *mūla-siddha*) destroys those born of one's lineage. A *siddha-sādhya* causes great affliction; a *sādhya-sādhya* causes extreme suffering. A *susiddha-sādhya* brings success through worship. An enemy of the *sādhya* (i.e., a *mūla-sādhya*) would take away one's well-being. A *siddha-susiddha* bestows the fruit of the higher path exactly as desired.

Through recitation (*japa*) and other practices, one will achieve success with a *susiddha* mantra; otherwise, it shall not be so. A *susiddha* mantra is one for which effort was exerted in a previous birth; therefore, one should employ that mantra for the accomplishment of all *siddhis*. An enemy *susiddha* mantra will certainly destroy one's entire lineage. An enemy *siddha* mantra kills one's son, while an enemy *sādhya* kills one's daughter. An enemy *susiddha* destroys one's wife, and an enemy *ari* (enemy) mantra brings about the death of the practitioner. In this matter of the "union of mantras" (*mantra-melana*), the names [of the mantras] as they are well-known should be taken when applying the combinations of *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth, especially during the transmission of a mantra.

One should take up a mantra whose name is "Siddha" (accomplished), according to the scriptural statement: "By which one who is asleep may wake. A mantra that brings little fault and many virtues should be accepted by the wise; once the eightfold status of "Siddha" and so forth is known, success (*siddhi*) arises from it. Now, regarding certain mantras for which the purification of "Siddha," "Sādhya," and so on has not been stated, the *Kulārṇava* says:

"In a single-syllable mantra, likewise in a *kūṭa*, in the leader of a *tripura* mantra, in one obtained in a dream, and in those belonging to Nṛsiṃha, Akavi, and Rāhu, as well as in the *Prāsāda* and the *Praṇava*, one should never purify them for 'Siddha' and the rest."

Furthermore, one should not purify the Siddha and other [categories] for mantras consisting of syllables that share the same *sapinda* (lineage). Thus it is stated in the *Somasiddhānta*: "The three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa*, the *Traipura*, *Caṇḍanāyaka*, the *Saura*, *Mṛtyuñjaya*, the *Śākta*, the *Śāmbhava*, the son of Vinatā (*Garuḍa*), those *Saura* mantras which are *Vaiṣṇava* and *Nārasiṃha*, as well as the *Praṇava*, the three-syllable [mantra], *Māyā*, the six-syllable *Vyomavyāpin*, and all *mālā-mantras*—one should never purify these regarding their status as *Siddha*, *Sādhya*, *Susiddha*, or *Ari*. Likewise, in the *Ratnasāgara*:

One should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories] of the eight-syllabled *Haṃsa*, nor likewise of the five-syllabled [mantra], nor of mantras with one, two, three, or more seed-syllables (*bīja*). One should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories] of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, Varāha, Kālikā, Siddhakālikā, Śyāmalā, and Caṇḍī. In the *Rudrayāmala*: "O Goddess of the Gods, O Pārvatī, in the Aghora mantra and in the Mālā mantra, one should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories] of a neuter mantra. In the *Kulamūlāvatāra*: "For a mantra taught in a dream, there is no rule at all."

And as for non-performance: having meditated upon the deity prescribed for one's own mantra, one should perform the recitation (*japa*); this becomes auspicious. In the *Agastya-saṃhitā*, regarding all the Rāma-mantras, listen, O bull among sages:

because they are the kings of mantras, one need not purify them of obstacles such as *siddha* and the rest. Those belonging to the Buddhists, Jains, Gopālas, and Vaiṣṇavas, which are devoid of the deliberations on *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*; the six-syllabled *Vyomavyāpin*; the *Mātṛkā*; the *Haravallabhā*; and the *Vahurūpa*—these five are considered common to all. Now, the initiation...

The time for initiation (*dīkṣā*): First, regarding the months, the *Manthānabhairava Tantra* states: "If initiation takes place in Caitra, it leads to suffering; in Vaiśākha, it bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*); in Jyeṣṭha, it would bring about death; in Āṣāḍha, it destroys one's kin; in Śrāvaṇa, it grants prosperity to men; in Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), it is considered to give suffering; in Āśvina, there shall be all accomplishments; in Kārtika, it grants an increase in knowledge; in Mārgaśīrṣa, it bestows auspiciousness; in Pauṣa, it destroys intelligence; in Māgha, there shall be the gain of gold; and in Phālguna, it bestows all accomplishments. Thus it is said.

In the month of Madhu (Caitra), there is suffering from the seizure of wealth; in Mādhava (Vaiśākha), there is a collection of jewels; in Jyeṣṭha, death occurs; and in Āṣāḍha, there is the destruction of kinsmen. In Śrāvaṇa, prosperity certainly arises; in Bhādrapada, there is loss. In the month of Āśvina, for the wise, there is indeed auspiciousness in every respect. In Kārttika, there is knowledge; in Mārgaśīrṣa, happiness also occurs. In Pauṣa, there is a decline of knowledge; in Māgha, there is an increase in intelligence; and in Phālguna, there is prosperity—one should avoid the intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Here, although in the month of Āśvina...

"Even if initiation (*dīkṣā*) is prescribed for that [time], nevertheless, by the statement of the *Śivayāmala*—'One who imparts a mantra on the Mahābhavacaturdaśī or during the eclipses of Āśvina shall remain poor for seven births'—the month of Āśvina, though prescribed for initiation, is not [recommended] as successful. Mahābhavacaturdaśī is Śivarātri. Likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*: 'O fair-faced one, on an auspicious day and under an auspicious weekday in the bright fortnight, one should begin the practice of mantras and so forth. Similarly, in the *Kālotara*: 'By those desiring liberation, [initiation should be taken] in the dark fortnight; by those desiring prosperity, [in the bright fortnight]. "

The *Śaivāgama* states: "The Great Goddess (Mahādevī) should always perform the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) during the bright fortnight, or as instructed by one's preceptor; in the bright fortnight there is total prosperity, while in the dark fortnight it is middling. Furthermore, regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the *Cintāmaṇi* says: "Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, the three *Uttara*s (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā), Hasta, Citrā, Svāti, Anurādhā (Maitra), Viśākhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Punarvasu, and Revatī are considered excellent for initiation. Anurādhā (Maitra) is likewise the 'Wish-Granting' (*Kāmadhenu*)."

The nine asterisms—Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, Hastaka, Svātī, Anurādhā, Revatī, and the three Uttarās—are auspicious for initiation (*dīkṣā*). Now, regarding the lunar days (*tithis*), the *Sārasaṃgraha* states: "The full moon, the fifth, the second, the seventh, the thirteenth, and the tenth are praised as granting all desires. In the *Śrīkaṇṭhasaṃhitā*, it is said: "The second and seventh are excellent; the sixth is censured in all cases; [initiation] may also be performed on the twelfth, and likewise on the third."
Furthermore, in the *Vijayāmālinī Tantra*, it is stated: "The tenth, the eleventh, the seventh, the thirteenth, and especially the twelfth of the bright fortnight [are auspicious].

In the *Ratnasāgara*: "The third is prescribed as always [auspicious], while the sixth is censured in all cases. On the seventh there is gain of wealth; on the eighth, the destruction of one's teacher;
on the ninth, the loss of property; the tenth bestows success (*siddhi*); on the eleventh there will be gain of wealth and of bulls; on the twelfth there will be gain of wealth."

On the thirteenth day there is great prosperity; on the fourteenth, the loss of disciples; the full moon (Pūrṇimā) grants success; on the new moon (Amāvāsyā), there is the destruction of sons; and the first lunar day (Pratipad) destroys the intellect. Now, regarding specific lunar days for specific deities, as stated in the *Kālottara*: the full moon is said to belong to Brahmā; the twelfth to the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu); the fourteenth to Śiva;
the thirteenth is declared to belong to Vāc (Sarasvatī); the second is said to belong to Śrī; the third to Pārvatī; the fourth to Gaṇanātha (Gaṇeśa); and the seventh to Bhānu (the Sun).

Alternatively, regarding the days of the week in the *Maṃtrasadbhāva*: when the commencement of a mantra occurs on Sunday or Friday, it is auspicious; specifically so on Wednesday and Thursday. On Saturday there is death, on Tuesday destruction, and on Monday everything is fruitless. In the *Vijayamālinītantra* it is said: "On Sunday one obtains intelligence; on Friday, the arrival of wealth; on Wednesday, freedom from fear; on Thursday, one becomes endowed with sons. On Saturday and Tuesday there is death, and on Monday there is ignorance. Now, as for the *yogas*, in the *Ratnāvalī* they are: *Prīti*, *Āyuṣmat*, *Saubhāgya*, *Śobhana*, *Śubha*, and *Sukarmā*.

Candhrati, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, Harṣaṇa, Varīyān, Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Raudra as the sixteenth. Now, regarding the ascendants (lagna) in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: the commencement of mantras and other rites in Aries bestows wealth and grain; in Taurus, one meets death; in Gemini, there is the loss of offspring; in Cancer, there is success in all matters; in Leo, there is the destruction of intelligence; in Virgo, it constantly bestows fortune (*lakṣmī*); in Libra, there are successes in all things; in Scorpio, there is success in all matters; in Sagittarius, there is the destruction of knowledge; and Capricorn...

Thus have been declared: Aquarius (Kumbha) bestows the increase of wealth, while Pisces (Mīna) always brings misery; such is the result of the zodiac signs. Now, regarding the auspicious and inauspicious results of planets situated in specific houses from the initiation ascendant (*dīkṣā-lagna*), as summarized in the *Manisārasaṃgraha*: "Malefic planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and benefic planets situated in the quadrants (*kendras*) and trines (*trikoṇas*), are all auspicious for initiation (*dīkṣā*); however, those situated in the eighth house cause total destruction. The eleventh house is the place of gain (*āya*); the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth houses are known as the quadrants (*kendras*); and the fifth... [text fragment ends].

The term *trikoṇa* (triple angle) refers to the fifth and ninth houses. Mercury joined with the malefic planets—the Sun, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—and the waning Moon are considered malefics (*pāpa*). Mercury not joined with Jupiter, Venus, or other malefics, as well as the full Moon, are auspicious (*śubha*). The eighth house is called *randhra*; the meaning is that all nine planets [occupying it] are malefics. Now, regarding the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*): therein, in the Śaiva Āgama, it is said: "In a favorable sign with its face downward, and especially when the Moon is pure, one should perform the contemplation of the beginning of one's own name during the strength of the lunar asterism (*tārābala*) in the dark fortnight. The morning time is the giver of dharma; the evening time is the giver of wealth and sovereignty."

It is traditionally taught that at midday all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are attained, while in the evening they become mediocre. However, the best of teachers have forbidden the imparting of mantras during the night. One should perform everything during the day; this is remembered as the supreme bestower of success. The asterisms (nakṣatras) whose faces are directed downwards are Mūla, Āgneya (Kṛttikā), Maghā, Bharaṇī, Sārpa (Āśleṣā), and the three Pūrvās. This group of nine constellations is proclaimed by the experts in astrology to be "downward-facing. In the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, pits, moats, excavations, and the laying of foundations, one should employ the Dhṛti yoga. Gambling and digging should be performed [under these conditions].

The commencement of the calculation of the *pūrveśa* (the eastern lord) is well known; likewise are the two deities (*dvideva*), Viśākhā, Āgneya (Kṛttikā), and Sārpa (Āśleṣā). Now, regarding the specific times for initiation (*dīkṣā*):

in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said that one should undertake the commencement of mantras and so forth during an eclipse of the moon or the sun. O Lord of Gods, the period following an eclipse lasts for seven days. Similarly, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*, it is stated:

"O Lord of Gods, on the festival of the sacred thread (*pavitraparva*), on the occasion of the offering of *damana* flowers (*dāmana* or *damanāropaṇa*), on an auspicious lunar day, at the time of an eclipse of the moon or the sun, at a holy pilgrimage site, or at Kurukṣetra... [The sentence continues].

Likewise, on the four *vīpīṭhas*, as well as during an eclipse of the sun or moon, on the *tantu* and *dāmana* parvas, and on the full-moon days (*parvaṇoḥ*), one who is undertaking initiation (*maṃtradīkṣā*) need not purify the months or the lunar days (*tithis*). Although it is stated here that the initiation occurs at the same time as the solar and lunar eclipses, nevertheless, those scriptural statements praising the [eclipse] should be understood as referring specifically to the solar eclipse; for at the time of a solar eclipse, nothing else need be sought, since the moon is not other than the sun at the time of the solar eclipse.

Furthermore, whatever is performed here [during a solar eclipse] shall yield infinite fruit. On the occasion of a solar eclipse (*sūryaparva*), there is no need for the purification of the month, lunar day, weekday, and so forth. At that time, a man may give or receive [mantras] from his guru; even without practice, the mantra becomes perfected (*siddhi*). This is because we see authoritative statements (*vacana*) prescribing specifically the solar eclipse for both the *Cintāmaṇi* and the *Kālikodbhava*. And as for the lunar eclipse: "The initiation (*dīkṣā*) which Janaka gave to those wandering in the forest—that initiation brings poverty in this very birth."

Because the *Svitiyoginītantra* contains a statement prohibiting initiation (*dīkṣā*) during a lunar eclipse, and because there is a previously cited statement prohibiting the imparting of mantras during the night, it should be understood that the time of a solar eclipse is also not highly recommended, as it is common to both types of eclipses. However, according to the words of Kolikodbhava: "During a lunar or solar eclipse, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a site of the Siddhas (*siddhakṣetra*), or in a temple of Śiva, the mere communication of the mantra is called 'instruction' (*upadeśa*)," this applies for the sake of curiosity to those who have been duly initiated into other mantras.

If there is a desire to receive a mantra, then even during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one may receive the mantra from one's own guru through oral instruction; thus, there is no fault in receiving the mantra at such times.

This concludes the section on the time for initiation (*dīkṣākāla*). Now, regarding the rosary (*japamālā*) according to the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*: it should be constructed from any one of the following materials—putrañjīva seeds, conch shell, coral, gems, crystal, pearl, lotus seeds, silver, gold, kuśa grass knots, or rudrākṣa beads—and consist of one hundred and eight, fifty-four, or twenty-seven beads, including a central bead (*meru*).

Now, regarding the time for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the rosary (*akṣamālā*): for Viṣṇu, it is the forenoon of the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*); for Śakti, it is the night of the eighth, ninth, or fourteenth; for Śiva, it is the thirteenth lunar day during the day; for Gaṇeśa, it is the fourteenth lunar day during the day; and for Sūrya, it is the seventh lunar day during the day. Regarding the threads for the rosary: for Viṣṇu, a lotus fiber (*padmasūtra*) or a silk thread (*kārpāsasūtra*) should be used; for Devī, a silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*); for Śiva, woolen thread (*ūrṇābhava*) or bark-fiber thread (*valkala*); and for Sūrya and Gaṇeśa, either cotton thread (*kārpāsasūtra*) or silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*).

If one should triple the number [of beads] made from *brahma-sūtra* (wool) or from the thread of a woman of the same caste as oneself, the thickness and measurement in other types of threads may be according to one's preference; this is the consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*). In that regard, having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—consisting of cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water—as well as clarified butter and sesame seeds for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*), the practitioner, having performed his daily obligatory rites and taken his meal in the morning, should at night wash the thread and the individual beads separately with the *pañcagavya* and water upon nine fresh *pippala* leaves.

Having placed the thread and the gems upon a base fashioned in the shape of a lotus, and having assigned the Praṇava, the syllable *Hrīṃ*, and the Mātṛkā letters [to them], one should worship the gems and the thread with perfumes and other offerings.

Then, having established the fire on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or similar site, one should perform oblations (*homa*) with sesame seeds mixed with ghee using the five mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta* according to one's capacity; if unable to perform the homa, one should perform recitation (*japa*). Having joined the mouth [of the thread] to the mouth [of the needle], one should pass the gems through it, and having tied a Brahma-knot (*brahmagraṃthi*) within each individual gem, one should string them together in the shape of a cow’s tail, making it thicker at all points.

Having joined two strings together with a single pearl of the same kind and strung them upon Mount Meru, one should wash [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and cool water while reciting the mantra: "I take refuge in Sadyojāta; obeisance to Sadyojāta! In every birth, in the primordial birth, favor me; obeisance to Bhavodbhava! Then, [one should wash it] with the mantra: "Obeisance to Vāmadeva, obeisance to Jyeṣṭha, obeisance to Rudra, obeisance to Kāla, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇa, obeisance to Balavikaraṇa, obeisance to Balapramathana, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamana."

Having anointed [the deity] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron while reciting the mantra "Oṃ namo manonmanāya namaḥ," and having offered incense made of agallochum, ushira-root, sugar, guggulu, honey, sandalwood, and clarified butter while reciting "Oṃ aghorebhyaḥ... rudrarūpebhyaḥ," one should apply an unguent of perfume, sandalwood, musk, saffron, and camphor while reciting "Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt. Thus one should smear [the image].

Then, with the mantra: "Oṃ, may Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, the Lord of all beings, the Sovereign of Brahmā, the Sovereign of the Brāhmaṇas, the Brahmā who is Śiva, be ever-auspicious to me, Oṃ," one should consecrate each seed-syllable (*bīja*) one hundred times. One should also consecrate Mount Meru with the mantra beginning "To the non-terrible ones" (*namo 'nantāghorebhyaḥ*). Then, having displayed the nine mudrās starting with the invocation (*āvāhana*), and having worshipped each seed-syllable with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using the five previously mentioned mantras, one should perform the *japa* of that [mantra] for as long as desired; this is the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).

The method for *drākṣā* (grapes) and similar items is as follows, and not otherwise. As for the method for other [materials]: having placed a strung garland in some vessel within its courtyard, one should separately invoke Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Durgā therein, worship them with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), and then, using the mantra "Hauṃ," pour *pañcagavya* over it.
Then, having lifted it from there, poured cool water over it, and washed it, one should anoint it with sandalwood, camphor, musk, saffron, and *aguru*. Upon that [garland], the "Hauṃ" mantra...

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, having worshipped the nine planets beginning with the Sun and the guardians of the directions beginning with Indra, and having offered oblations according to one's capacity with sesame seeds mixed with ghee while reciting the root mantra— (as stated in the *Maṃtracaṃdrakā*,
page 85, verse 2700).
